articles.title: Severely ill ICE detainees targeted for imminent deportation in Florida, advocates say
articles.summary:
Flights to unknown countries in Africa are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail

Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two

blocks.text: Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.
The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions have been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.
“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband has been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa’.

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway’. We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”
Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.
Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.
“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details.
Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks, and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump’s massive second term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.
The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

articles.title: Family of prison officer killed by IRA receives state apology
articles.summary: Brian Stack was crossing a street in Dublin in 1983 when he was shot in the back of the neck and died 18 months later.

blocks.text: Image source, Handout
Brian Stack was shot in the back of the neck as he left a boxing match in 1983
ByFiona Murray
BBC News NI
The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA has received a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing.
Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck.
Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49.
There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing.
Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin offered an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the Dáil (Irish parliament).
Stack's wife Sheila and her sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver were in the Dáil chamber for the apology.
Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" on this case.
Apology means 'an awful lot'
Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme Brian Stack's son, Austin Stack, said the apology "means an awful lot to us".
"It's a great sense of comfort, to particularly my mother and to myself and my two brothers, because the state is officially owning up to the errors and the missions that happened," he said.
He went on to say that the serious crime review team looked into the first investigation and "they found 194 errors and omissions".
"So I have, and my family have, met with several ministers for justice down through the years and we have a requested sight of that report.
"And every time we've requested it, we've been told that it's an internally valid document and that we cannot see it."
Austin Stack said that Wednesday would be a very emotional day for his family.
"My dad was doing a very difficult job at a very difficult time in our history," he said.
"He was awarded the Irish Prison Service's highest bravery award for that work that he was doing. And this is further vindication of him and his good name."
Prior to the Dáil proceedings, the Stack family held a private meeting at government buildings with the taoiseach and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan.
'Utterly unacceptable'

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taoiseach Micheál Martin formally apologised to the Stack family

blocks.text: Image source, PA Media
Taoiseach Micheál Martin formally apologised to the Stack family
In 2007 the Garda Commissioner directed a review of the case by the Garda Serious Crime Review Team. Over 200 recommendations were made relating to the cases.
This review led to "serious failings" being found as well as "the shortcomings in the management" of the earlier Garda investigation.

These failures, listed by Martin in the Dáil, are: failure to keep a map made of the crime scene, a failure to keep a motorbike helmet found near the crime scene and linked to the crime, a failure to keep custody of material exhibits, including various fingerprints, samples and debris gathered during the investigation.

The taoiseach also said there was a failure to document some potentially important aspects of the original investigation, including whether Brian's colleagues at Portlaoise Prison were interviewed and whether prisoners at the prison were interviewed.
There was also a failure to interview the Stack family and to interview Brian's wider group of friends.
"It is plainly and utterly unacceptable that material that was potentially of evidential value to the investigation can no longer be located by An Garda Síochána.
"It is admitted by An Garda Síochána that these are serious matters that had an impact on the investigation," Martin said.
"As Taoiseach, and on behalf of the Government, I want to formally apologise to the Stack family for these failings."

blocks.caption: Image caption, NI secretary Sir Chris Bryant was asked about the matter in the House of Commons

blocks.text: NI secretary Sir Chris Bryant was asked about the matter in the House of Commons
Speaking in the Commons during Northern Ireland questions on Wednesday, Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said he "warmly welcomed" the taoiseach making the apology.

Asked about the matter by Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson, Sir Chris said Dublin doing so was "entirely right and proper" and went to the heart of discussions MPs had been having this week as they debated the government's Troubles legacy bill.
He added that it was "incumbent on all of us to make fulsome and not mealy-mouthed apologies".
'Regret'
The IRA admitted killing Stack in 2013 after his family mounted a long campaign to secure the admission, and met Sinn Féin's Gerry Adams and a former IRA commander.
Adams, at that time, expressed his "regret" to the Stack family over the killing.
A Sinn Féin spokesperson said that "in a 2013 statement, a former IRA leader acknowledged that IRA volunteers were responsible for Brian Stack's killing".

"The statement said the shooting had not been authorised by the IRA leadership, accepted IRA responsibility for his death, said it should not have happened and expressed sorrow for the pain and hurt suffered by the family."

The spokesperson added: "As republicans, we acknowledge the hurt caused by republican actions. That suffering cannot be disowned. We are sorry for all the lives lost during the period of conflict on this island, without exception."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee said the Provisional IRA "are responsible"

blocks.text: Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee said the Provisional IRA "are responsible"
Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee also spoke during the State apology, she said: "The State failed you during their investigation into Brian's killing."
She said Brian was "targeted" by the Provisional IRA and said "they are responsible".

"To Sheila and to all of the Stack family, we are deeply sorry for all that you have endured, for the failures of the investigation and the additional suffering they have caused you, we are deeply sorry. I hope today's formal apology brings some measure of peace and comfort."
Donegal Sinn Féin TD (member of Irish parliament) Pearse Doherty said the Stack's family "long search for answers deserves respect".
"No apology can restore Brian Stack's life or return the years spent seeking answers but it can recognise the wrong done."
He said the failures of the garda investigation "compounded" the suffering of the Stack family.
In 2019, the family received an apology from then garda commissioner Drew Harris in relation to the handling of the investigation into the murder.
In 2023, gardaí told the family that the file on the case - which was with the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions) - was being sent back to police for further investigation.
Stack was the only prisoner officer in the state killed by violence related to the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

articles.title: Israeli military detains US politician Brad Lander and rabbis at olive harvest
articles.summary:
About 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers held near Nahalin in West Bank and taken to police station

The Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping…

blocks.text: The Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general.

“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers,” Lander posted from a bus taking him to a police station. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nahalin in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”

Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist. He believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot be a true democracy while it denies Palestinians their human rights and freedom.
Allow content provided by a third party?

This article includes content hosted on platform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.
An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Lander’s critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his resounding primary victory against Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel.

He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide.
Settler militants have unleashed extreme violence on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives from their trees across the occupied West Bank, and anyone accompanying them.

A vicious assault on a US photojournalist and attacks on European diplomats and a French mayor over the weekend drew international condemnation and calls for the Israeli government to crack down on militants.
Wednesday’s olive-picking from trees outside the village of Nahalin was uneventful until a large contingent of Israeli security forces arrived, the organisers Protect the Harvest said in a statement.

“All volunteers were peacefully harvesting on the private land of a Palestinian family who had invited them. For reasons that remain unclear, the Israeli army showed up and detained approximately 80 people who were present.”

Soldiers said the area had been declared a closed military zone, separated the group by nationality and drove them to a nearby police station in minibuses for the Israelis and a larger bus for Americans.
Joshua Schoffman, who served as Israel’s deputy attorney general for more than a decade, described the mass detention as a “complete hallucination” in a post on social media.

“Just now, they told me that I’m being detained for the crime of olive harvesting,” he wrote. “We were asked to stop, and everyone complied. There was no friction whatsoever with settlers or with the security forces.”

Lander was released with a warning but all the others were still being held, Protect the Harvest said. Detainees include Jill Jacobs, the chief executive of T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, and 11 other American rabbis affiliated with the group.
The detainees have been given water but no food. The Israeli military and police did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Monday, Lander made a first post about his journey to Palestine. “Our goals for the trip are to help protect the olive harvest – and to shed a light on the reality of the occupation,” he wrote. “Thankfully, our corner of today’s harvest was peaceful and successful. But violence unfortunately is never far away.”

articles.title: ICC Prosecution removes one incident in trial brief vs. Duterte
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) Prosecution removed one incident from its trial brief against former president Rodrigo Duterte following the Trial Chamber"s order.

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 9:25pm
The International Criminal Court (ICC) Prosecution removed one incident from its trial brief against former president Rodrigo Duterte following the Trial Chamber’s order.

The ICC Prosecution and Duterte’s defense team have been discussing the evidence that the former has submitted ahead of the official opening of the trial on November 30. Duterte’s defense team has raised several concerns about the prosecution’s evidence, including its large volume.

“The Prosecution hereby provides an updated version of its Trial Brief filed 4 September 2026 (‘Trial Brief’) and Annexes C.1 and C.2 thereto, further to the Chamber's order to remove Incident 57 from the incidents included in the Trial Brief,” the prosecution said in a document from the ICC.
The ICC prosecution did not publicly disclose which case this was, as it contained sensitive information relating to witnesses.
Following the Chamber’s orders, the Prosecution said that it removed all references to Incident 57 in the Trial Brief, replacing them with “[DELETED]" to be able to cross-reference it.
“No amendments have been made to the Prosecution's List of Witnesses or its List,” the prosecution said.
According to the prosecution panel, other incidents relating to Incident 57 still had contextual elements of crimes against humanity and Duterte’s supposed criminal responsibility.
The document was signed by acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang.
Duterte is detained at the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands, for crimes against humanity in relation to the drug war.
The drug war saw at least 6,000 people dead, with rights groups believing that the number could be as high as 30,000. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Thousands of California public employees set to strike over contract
articles.summary:
SEIU Local 1000, representing nurses and teachers, pushing for higher wages, telework and affordable healthcare

Thousands of

blocks.text: Thousands of California state workers were set to strike on Wednesday, rallying outside government buildings in several cities, as tensions boiled over lapsed contract negotiations with Governor Gavin Newsom’s administration.
SEIU Local 1000, a union that represents roughly 100,000 public employees, including nurses and teachers, has been pushing for higher wages, flexible telework and affordable healthcare.
The union has been at an impasse with the state since its contract expired on 30 June.

SEIU Local 1000’s negotiators say state officials rejected their key proposals: a 20% salary increase over three years, higher state healthcare contributions and flexible telework – Newsom has required state workers to be in office four days a week.

Union representatives also argued in a complaint filed with California’s public employment relations board that the state engaged in bad faith bargaining, by allegedly waiting until 30 June to respond to some of the proposals and saying there was “no money” for additional compensation.
The state has not commented publicly on the status of the contract negotiations, citing confidentiality.
A spokesperson for Newsom’s office did not immediately comment on the work stoppage.
Wednesday’s picketing marked a first for the union.

California’s department of human resources (CalHR) had reportedly attempted to block the strike, arguing the union did not have plans to exempt essential workers and thus was compromising public health and safety. The labor board determined a list of about 5,000 workers deemed essential, according to the union, who will report to work during the strike.

articles.title: Double blow to Healey as inflation rises to 3.5% and monthly deficit hits £24bn
articles.summary: Consumer prices rise by more than expected while government’s debt interest payments surge to record high for September

blocks.text: Inflation surged to 3.5% last month while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn, in a double dose of bad news for John Healey before next week’s budget.

The Office for National Statistics said annual inflation rose from 3.1% in August, overshooting City forecasts of a rise in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 3.4%, as a result of the surging cost of fuel.
Oil and gas prices have soared since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, throttling gas and oil flows through the strait of Hormuz.
Rising inflation has also contributed to higher government borrowing costs – the key factor behind the deterioration in the public finances since the spring statement in March.
Official figures show the government paid £10.9bn in debt interest last month: the highest September figure since records began, and only the eighth time the monthly number has been above £10bn.
Payments on some government bonds rise in line with inflation. The ONS said higher inflation had added £4bn to debt interest costs in September alone.
Total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time – although as a share of the size of the economy it has fallen to 94%, from 95% a year ago.

In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing is £97.8bn, the ONS said – £4.4bn lower than last year, but still £6bn higher than the independent Office for Budget Responsibility had expected.
The twin pieces of bad news underline the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.

The ONS said a rise in the cost of motor fuels was the single largest factor pushing up inflation in September. The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p a litre from August compared with a fall of 0.2p in the same period last year.

Diesel, which is often refined in the Middle East, rose by 10.7p a litre last month compared with a fall of 0.4p a litre in September 2025. Air fares, which are heavily affected by the price of fuel, dropped in September by much less than usual after the traditional summer peak.
In better news for the chancellor, the cost of clothing fell slightly and food prices growth remained steady at 1.3% as competition among supermarkets offset increases in transport costs.

Rising prices make it even more likely that Bank of England officials will raise interest rates from their current 3.7% level when they meet next month. Rate setters are concerned that inflation will jump above 4% next year as the price of a wider range of goods increases in response to higher oil and gas prices.

September’s reading commits the chancellor to raising most working-age welfare benefit payments from next April by more than expected. For instance, the 3.5% rise will uprate weekly child benefit by 95p to £28 for the first child.
after newsletter promotion

It also means a bigger than forecast inflation-linked rise in business rates in England. The tax firm Ryan said this could raise more than £1bn in extra receipts for the Treasury and would be paid mostly by organisations in the hospitality, leisure, education, health, transport and utility sectors.

September’s CPI reading came in lower than the 3.9% wage growth figure for the three months to July, meaning that the state pension will almost certainly rise by the latter figure under the formula that dictates the triple lock.

Healey blamed the inflation rise on the war in the Gulf. “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide,” he said, adding that his budget would “drive for growth in every postcode” to improve living standards.

Charlotte O’Leary, an economist at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said the run of three months of rising annual inflation was likely to continue through the winter, even if there was some resolution to the conflict in the Middle East.

“Higher fuel and transport costs will likely push up food prices, and January’s large price cap increase will land as household energy demand peaks. Given this, inflation could reach 4%, double the Bank of England’s target, by early 2027,” she said.

Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultancy WPI, said the higher than expected inflation rate meant it was almost inevitable that Bank of England officials would raise interest rates when they met on 5 November, but he cautioned against persistent rises in the cost of borrowing.
“Raising interest rates cannot produce more oil or gas, and further tightening risks weakening an already fragile economy,” he said.

articles.title: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets
articles.summary: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests

blocks.text: France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.
With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots,a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate - on bonds issued by the second-largest economy in the eurozone.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat), issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%.
The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks.

Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes, evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living.
Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities.
Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters also set fire to the town hall in Limoges.
No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024.
The parliamentary gridlocked has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 years old and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending.

France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action.
International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”.
after newsletter promotion
Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer period loans.
Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies.
“The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said.

“It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”

articles.title: UK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See Everything
articles.summary:
Tickets for film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes said to be selling out after $15m opening weekend in the US

It is the film everyone seems to be talking about, spawning memes and…
articles.byline: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent

blocks.text: It is the film everyone seems to be talking about, spawning memes and fuelling feverish online debate about its subject, the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.

Now, a month before Nathan Fielder’s documentary You Can See Everything reaches UK cinemas, tickets for screenings are already selling out after its remarkable $15m (£11.3m) opening weekend in the US.
Clare Binns, the creative director of Picturehouse Cinemas, said the excitement was reminiscent of the response to Greta Gerwig’s Barbie, which became a global box-office phenomenon in 2023.
“People are hungry in a way that we haven’t really seen since then,” she said. “And for it to be a three-hour documentary, it’s bonkers.”

blocks.caption: Elizabeth Holmes is questioned by Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything. Photograph: Courtesy of A24

blocks.text: Tickets for the film, which opens in the UK on 20 November, went on sale at Picturehouse Central in London before its US opening, Binns said, and demand has prompted the chain to add extra screenings. At the Ritzy in Brixton, the first screen had almost sold out, leading the cinema to sell tickets for a showing at a second.
“It’s fantastic, it proves again that there’s a different kind of audience coming to the cinema,” Binns said. “They came to see Backrooms, they came to see Obsession, they came to see NAZA.

“There’s a real appetite for smart films that talk to an audience differently than the studios have talked to them before. With this documentary, you’ve got a story that has been mined to some extent with the Dropout and podcasts. But I think the fact that Nathan Fielder spent a month with Elizabeth Holmes is a huge draw. He’s a smart guy, and audiences want something they can relate to.”
Cineworld has also reported strong demand. Stuart Crane, its international vice-president of content, said “the speed and scale of demand has been remarkable”.

Initial screenings at Cineworld Leicester Square sold out after tickets went on sale at about 40 cinemas on Sunday. The chain has since added more screenings at Leicester Square and expanded bookings to a further 35 cinemas nationwide.

Vue has reported similar excitement. Dean Cross, its senior screen content manager, said it was “seeing incredible buzz both within the industry and amongst cinemagoers”, and it was “particularly encouraging to see a documentary capturing the attention of younger audiences”.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes at a federal prison camp in Bryan, Texas. Photograph: Adrees Latif/Reuters

blocks.text: The momentum for You Can See Everything has been building since it was unveiled at a secret screening at the Telluride film festival in Colorado in September, where audiences were required to surrender their phones. A teaser trailer released the same day quickly went viral, with Holmes herself joining the online conversation, responding to tweets about the film and its trailer.

Co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the film has won widespread critical acclaim. The Guardian described it as “a modern masterpiece of deceit”, praising its unsettling exploration of Holmes and the blurred boundaries between documentary and performance.
Its US opening was the biggest for a documentary in more than 20 years, with more than 2,000 screenings selling out at 855 cinemas. More than 70% of its opening-weekend audience was under 35.

“People want to enjoy films in a cinema with other people,” Binns said. “The younger demographic want shared experiences. They want to talk about it with their friends, and you can’t do that when you’re sitting on your own watching a TV.
“Cinema has been ruled out so many times. Covid, the rise of streamers. Everybody is aware cinema has to change, it has to offer customers something different. But never rule us out.”

articles.title: House members urge Marcos to seek Chinese envoy Jing Quan's recall
articles.summary: Ten members of the House of Representatives called on Pres. Marcos, Jr. to declare Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata or ask China to recall him, over his reference to using force.

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 8:56pm

Ten members of the House of Representatives called on President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos, Jr. to declare Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, or ask China to recall him, over his reference to using force in relation to the Philippines.

Lawmakers led by House Senior Deputy Minority Leader Leila de Lima made the call under House Resolution 1562, saying it is in line with the Philippines’ position which renounces war as an instrument of national policy, adopts the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the land and adheres to the policy of peace, equality, justice, freedom, cooperation, and amity with all nations.

“On October 15, 2026, when asked about Secretary of National Defense Gilberto C. Teodoro Jr.'s characterization of China as a regional 'troublemaker,' Ambassador Jing Quan, speaking before reporters at the Diliman Dialogues in Quezon City, declared, 'If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not use force,' further remarking that the Philippines should consider itself fortunate to have China as a neighbor because Beijing would not resort to force because it loved peace,” the Resolution read.

“Under the Constitution, the President, being vested with executive power, holds primary authority to conduct foreign relations and to represent the nation in its dealings with other states and must, therefore, take decisive action in response to statements and conduct that undermine national sovereignty and threaten the country's security,” the Resolution added.

In addition, the lawmakers cited that the Chinese Embassy in Manila addressed the members of the Senate and the House of Representatives who proposed declaring Ambassador Jing persona non grata for the aforementioned statements, daring the members of the Philippine Congress to "Just do it” and accused Filipino reporters and politicians of "exaggeration, taking things out of context, and creating hype.”

“These incidents demonstrate China's disregard for the sovereign rights of the Philippines and underscore the inconsistency between the Chinese Government's words and its actions. Now, therefore, be it resolved, that the House of Representatives urge the President of the Philippines to declare Ambassador Jing Quan of the People's Republic of China persona non grata, or, in the alternative, to request his recall by the Government of the People's Republic of China,” the Resolution said.
Other co-authors of the Resolution include:

articles.title: Woman told she had cancer by NHS worker who inappropriately accessed her records
articles.summary:
Pippa Boardman said she lost her dignity through data breach at Royal Cornwall hospital by man she barely knew

A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee she barely knew who had…

blocks.text: A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee she barely knew who had accessed her medical records days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.
Pippa Boardman said she lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall hospital in Truro.
Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said her personal information was accessed by a man she knew only vaguely who worked at the hospital.

She said: “I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play. This man said to me: ‘Pippa, I don’t want you to worry, but you’ve got cancer.’ I just couldn’t really believe it.”
Two days later, Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer.

Boardman, who is recovering well from the cancer, said Royal Cornwall’s handling of the case had reinforced her trauma, and she said the trust only apologised once it had been contacted by reporters at the BBC.
She told the BBC: “It really distresses me people can’t see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately.”

A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall hospitals trust said: “We are truly sorry that Ms Boardman was contacted in this way. Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her and discuss her diagnosis. This should not have happened, and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused.

“Appropriate action was taken following our investigation, which was carried out immediately after Ms Boardman raised her concern. While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously.

“We have reminded all our staff of their responsibility to protect patient confidentiality and that records must only ever be accessed for a legitimate work-related reason. We are also reviewing our policies and processes in light of the strengthened NHS England guidance on inappropriate access to patient information.
“We sincerely apologise to Ms Boardman for what happened and for the time she has had to wait for answers.”

articles.title: Student who stabbed housemate to death in Gloucestershire jailed for life
articles.summary:
Zack Coughlan, 23, killed Jamie Collins, 21, in garden of home they shared and initially denied murder

A university student who lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing…

blocks.text: A university student who lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing him 30 times has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 28 years.
Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed in black and wore a mask and gloves to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home in Filton, South Gloucestershire.
Bristol crown court heard Collins was stabbed repeatedly and Coughlan left him dying in an alleyway as he cycled away on his housemate’s bike.
Coughlan had denied murder and a trial was under way at Bristol crown court but he changed his plea to guilty on Tuesday.
Sentencing Coughlan on Wednesday, Mr Justice Linden said: “He [Collins] was caught totally unaware by you and was utterly defenceless.”
He dismissed Coughlan’s evidence in court that Collins had previously threatened him, describing Collins as a “gentle soul”.
The judge said no one would know why Coughlan killed Collins.
Collins was attacked shortly before 6pm on 8 April this year after cycling home from University of the West of England (UWE) Bristol where he was studying robotics alongside his killer.
Adam Vaitilingam KC, prosecuting, told the jury: “This was a carefully planned and cold-blooded execution.”
Coughlan dumped the bike at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing in a pond, in carrier bags weighed down with bricks.
He returned to the house they shared at about 9pm, put a pizza in the oven and did some online gaming with friends.
At around 2am, Coughlan dialled 999 claiming he had just found Collins’s body in the garden.
The attack was caught on CCTV installed at the house they shared, which Coughlan showed the attending police officers who initially treated him as a witness.
The defendant’s blood had been found on Collins’s bike, and analysis of his mobile phone matched the killer’s movements afterwards captured on CCTV.
Coughlan also had injuries to his hands, and he told people who saw him bleeding that he had been climbing trees and had fallen and hurt himself.
After the murder, Coughlan told a university friend he wanted to hold a memorial for his housemate.
Coughlan and Collins, originally from Swansea, were both final year students and lived together in a £300,000 three-bedroom house owned by the defendant.
The defendant is half Danish and grew up with his family in Cork, Ireland, before moving to Bristol to study robotics at the age of 19.
In a statement issued following Coughlan’s change of plea, Collins’s family said his death had “affected our family in a deep, profound, and lasting way”.

“As a family we have had to explain repeatedly to people what has happened,” they said. “Every time we do so it reinforces the pain of him having been killed so suddenly, and in such a senseless and brutal way.
“Our family has been sickened that Zack Coughlan pretended to help Jamie when in fact he is responsible for killing him.”

articles.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case linked to East Africa
articles.summary: The female patient, who sources have told the BBC is not Nigerian, is in isolation and in an Abuja hospital.
articles.byline: Simi Jolaoso, Makuochi Okafor, Patrick Jackson, Mansur Abubakar

blocks.text: Nigeria has recorded a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda in East Africa to Abuja, capital of the West African state.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the diagnosis had been confirmed by laboratory tests.
The patient, who health sources have told the BBC is not Nigerian and is the wife of a diplomat, is in isolation and receiving medical care after being admitted to a hospital in Abuja.
She developed symptoms on Wednesday 7 October, four days after arriving in the country, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Health authorities have begun contact-tracing to prevent further spread, with 44 close contacts of the woman identified.
Nigeria, the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East Africa, successfully stopped a previous outbreak in 2014.
Uganda's Ministry of Health has stressed there are currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country.
"We urge the public to remain calm, vigilant and to practice regular handwashing and sanitising," it said.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external.
It was caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.
Following the latest case in Nigeria, Uganda's health ministry said preliminary information indicated that the patient had transited through Uganda without symptoms.

In a statement on X, Uganda's Director General of Health Services Charles Olaro said the woman had travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.
He said her symptoms had only developed after arriving in Nigeria.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
The woman's exact travel history - key to tracing contacts - appears to be unclear at the moment.

"The location of exposure remains under investigation. The government of Nigeria is yet to provide detailed information on her travel itinerary and clinical history which will guide further investigations and any necessary contact tracing," Olaro said.
Nigeria's health minister confirmed the woman had had no symptoms when she arrived in Nigeria, but he said the patient had not confirmed travel to DR Congo.
"We presume that it was likely picked in Uganda," Pate told the national broadcaster Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) on Tuesday evening.
Her travel documents will be used to trace contacts and the authorities have urged the public to co-operate with health officials carrying out contact tracing.
The disease has also recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.
On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.
Since the outbreak, Nigeria has stepped up disease surveillance, with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control issuing public health advice to travellers.
The agency says travellers from countries with active or relevant Ebola transmission may be required to complete a health declaration form. Those arriving from other countries are currently exempt.
It has also urged travellers to remain vigilant and seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms of Ebola.
In 2014, Nigeria managed to beat an outbreak of Ebola which caused at least eight deaths.

articles.title: Trump suggests he could be ‘arbitrator’ in DoJ anti-fraud whistleblower scheme
articles.summary:
President makes suggestion while announcing new program to reward tipsters who submit fraud allegations

Donald Trump suggested on Tuesday that

blocks.text: Donald Trump suggested on Tuesday that he would serve as “the arbitrator” of decisions in the justice department’s new anti-fraud program that awards compensation to those who submit tips resulting in conviction or significant federal enforcement.

While announcing the new program alongside JD Vance, the vice-president, who leads the White House’s taskforce to eliminate fraud, the president told reporters he had a solution for situations where multiple people submit a tip for the same alleged fraud.
“I was just thinking, when you do these things, sometimes there’s a dispute as to who turned ’em in and who didn’t turn ’em in, who’s supposed to get what and when, you know,” Trump told reporters.

“So I am going to do something, which I think people will like, I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions. In other words, I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous, believe me,” the US president said, resulting in laughter from the group.

It is unclear whether Trump was being genuine about his new role. The Department of Justice website says the department has “sole discretion” in issuing rewards and exercising its authority in the program.
When asked whether the president’s statement was true, the White House referred the Guardian to Trump’s Oval Office comments.
The Guardian has asked the justice departmentfor comment.
The new fraud whistleblower incentive program gives anyone who submits a tip the opportunity to receive a financial reward of up to $30,000 for tips in the “charging stage of a criminal case”.

The government already gives financial rewards to whistleblowers who file lawsuits against individuals and companies committing financial fraud through the False Claims Act. If the government intervenes in a suit and prosecutes it, whistleblowers can obtain 15% to 25% of the financial penalties.
Vance said the new program differs from the False Claims Act because it expands the opportunity for financial reward in cases of fraud related to the government.
“Over 99% of the fraud that we’re finding in the federal government isn’t covered by the False Claims Act,” Vance said.
The new program also provides whistleblower rewards at an earlier stage of investigation, rather than requiring it to result in large fines or forfeiture.

Vance said he and Trump decided to create the program to incentivize more people to report fraud like Nick Shirley, a conservative influencer who went viral earlier this year for accusing Somali-run childcare centers in Minnesota of rampant fraud.

During his Oval Office announcement, Trump indicated the program would result in whistleblowers obtaining 1% of however much fraud was uncovered, insisting people could make “millions and millions” of dollars from submitting tips.
However, the justice department website says the program is limited to a $30,000 reward.

“You’ll get your money immediately, but I’ll make the determination,” Trump added. “So if two people are fighting over it, maybe they’ll split it or maybe whatever, but I’ll make that determination. It’ll be done expeditiously and fairly.”

Trump encouraged members of the media to participate in the program by investigating and reporting instances of fraud. He said the government would be willing to give reporters the financial reward, so long as their respective outlet allowed it.
“We’re going to let the reporters partake because you know a lot of things that are happening,” Trump said.

articles.title: State attorneys general step up plans to counter Trump’s meddling in midterms
articles.summary:
Coordination by Democratic officials overseeing elections includes Zoom calls and in-person tabletop exercises

Democratic state attorneys general, other top state officials and civic groups…

blocks.text: Democratic state attorneys general, other top state officials and civic groups have accelerated planning to thwart any federal meddling in the November midterm elections by Donald Trump as he continues his false charges of widespread voting fraud and veiled threats of interfering in the process.

Since early this year, 24 Democratic attorneys general have expanded coordination with about a dozen Democratic secretaries of state and several civic groups using weekly Zoom calls and in-person tabletop exercises to strategize about countering any federal intervention in the elections.

The enhanced cooperation is significant because secretaries of state are responsible for supervising elections and state state attorneys general are charged with defending the laws governing them. The coordination efforts by the state officials are being spearheaded by the Progressive State Leaders Committee (PSLC), the public policy arm of the Democratic Attorneys General Association.

The Democratic attorneys general say they are especially worried about interference in the elections by the Department of Justice and other parts of the Trump administration given the president’s repeated false charges of rampant voting fraud in US elections.
On Trump’s first day in office last January, he falsely called the 2020 election “rigged” and has made similar claims hundreds of times since he lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden.

Nick Brown, the Washington state attorney general, said that the justice department and the Trump administration were “the biggest adversary to a smooth election”. Brown added that “Trump lies about the election on a regular basis. Truth is not a goal of his. That creates a whole host of concerns for us.”

The Department of Justice, for instance, announced dubious plans this summer to deploy 1,000 poll monitors, which prompted the NAACP to file a lawsuit on 4 October seeking details of how the monitors will be deployed; by comparison, in 2022 the justice department deployed 289 monitors, according to CBS news.

In another worrisome move, the justice department has sued 30 states to obtain their unredacted voter lists that contain sensitive personal information. Democratic attorneys general have been involved in challenging the justice department lawsuits, and the justice department has lost 26 of the lawsuits that courts have ruled on.

Furthermore, Harmeet Dhillon, who heads the justice department’s civil rights division, this summer wrote to state election officials threatening prosecutions if they didn’t cooperate adequately in hunting for voting fraud.

To counter threats of federal intervention in the November elections, Brown has led the weekly Zoom calls with PSLC partners including offices of secretaries of state and key civil society groups such as the Democracy Defenders Fund, the States United Democracy Center and the Brennan Center for Justice.

A former US attorney and federal prosecutor, Brown said the Zoom calls focus on election security issues in general and potential event scenarios –including the possibility of ICE agents showing up near some polling places and ballots being seized in some races.

Brown, who chairs the PSLC election-protection working group, also led two “tabletop” in-person exercises in Milwaukee in May and Detroit in September that included attenders from secretary of state offices and other PSLC partners.

Besides these efforts, Brown’s office co-led the legal moves that blocked Trump’s radical plans in his March executive order to overhaul and curb voting by mail, which the supreme court ruled against last month.

The fears of federal meddling in the elections have been fueled by Trump’s drumbeat of baseless allegations about large-scale noncitizen voting and voting-by-mail fraud, both of which the president falsely alleged in a nationalized televised address on 16 July.
In his TV speech, Trump made the factually inaccurate claim that noncitizen voting, which has long been illegal and historically rare, poses a “crisis of election security”.
Trump’s fixation with portraying noncitizen voting as a crisis has been significantly undercut by data from the conservative Heritage Foundation, which cited just 100 cases over a 25-year period.

Other concerns about federal meddling in the next elections were spurred by Trump’s comments to the New York Times that he regrets not calling out the national guard to seize ballots in the 2020 election, and his urging Republicans last month at a mini convention in Texas to “cheat like hell like they do”.
Oregon’s attorney general, Dan Rayfield, shares Brown’s concerns about the threat to the elections posed by Trump.

“From day one, Trump has been taking dead aim at our elections,” Rayfield said, “We’re trying to dispute some of the misinformation that the Trump administration keeps putting out,” including about the dangers of voting by mail.
Oregon, he noted, was the first state to adopt all voting by mail and has had two GOP secretaries of state in the last decade who have been happy with the voting system.

Elsewhere, Arizona’s Democratic secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, whose office has participated in a number of the Zoom calls and the two tabletop exercises, said the increasing cooperation this year with the attorneys general represents “an all-hands approach” to cope with the threats of federal interference. “We have an adversary we didn’t expect in the form of this administration.”
Fontes added that a central concern of his office was that the administration’s “constant drumbeat of lies is going to suppress the vote”.
The Democratic attorney general efforts have benefited from the input of several non-partisan groups.

Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund who participated in the Milwaukee and Detroit tabletop exercises and has been on some of the Zoom calls, praised the the work of the attorneys general preparing to combat federal election meddling.

“The pro-democracy AGs are preparing for anything that this anti-voter administration may throw at them,” said Eisen, a former special counsel for ethics and government reform to Barack Obama. “The level of preparation by the AGs and the secretaries of state is off the charts.”

More broadly, Larry Norden, an elections expert with the Brennan Center who has participated in a handful of the Zoom calls and the two tabletop strategy exercises organized by the PSLC, warned: “Leaders in the administration, including at the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security, have repeatedly threatened or attempted to exert control over the midterm elections.”

Norden noted that “for the last 18 months, they have been met by pushback and consistently lost. I don’t expect that to change in the coming weeks, but everyone involved in this fight knows we must continue to be prepared.”

To better protect election results and bolster coordination between the Democratic attorneys general and Democratic secretaries of state, two new groups were created in 2026. One of them is called the AGSOS Election Protection Pac, and it’s working to raise funds to elect more Democrats to both state offices, and the other is dubbed AGSOS Election Protection Action, which serves as a policy arm.

Addressing the PSLC work to counter Trump administration election interference threats, Sean Rankin, the president of the Democratic Attorneys General Association, noted that “it is a concern that the administration will try to seize ballots and the AGs and secretaries of state are working on responses to that to find solutions if that happens”.

Mai Ratakonda, a top election-protection attorney with the States United Democracy Center, stressed that since the justice department early this year in a highly unusual move seized 2020 ballots from Fulton county, Georgia, election officials are “ready and prepared to respond” to the threat of ballots being seized in the midterms.
More broadly, Rayfield cautioned that Trump “continues to take steps to interfere in our elections … This president has stretched our democracy more than any president in my lifetime.”

articles.title: As fans reject AI-generated music, even boosters are drawing the line
articles.summary:
Enthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselves

Streaming services, notable musicians and fans are confronting the growing…

blocks.text: Streaming services, notable musicians and fans are confronting the growing presence of AI-generated music and drawing lines in the sand.
On Tuesday, Spotify announced it had removed some 50m songs considered AI slop from its recommendations to users over the past year.

“Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” a statement from the company read. Spotify requires “AI persona” badges on artist profiles that don’t represent a real human being, but it does not require individual songs generated by AI to be labeled. Other streaming services have taken more stringent stances.

Though it’s cracking down on slop tracks, Spotify is far from AI-shy. The company allows users to create playlists with generative AI and has promised a tool for making AI-generated remixes and cover songs.

Unable to ignore the tide, even early AI boosters like the singer and producer Grimes, former paramour of Elon Musk and mother to three of his 14 children, have declared their limits on allowable amounts of AI. She and other musicians say they are open to AI-generated music but wary.

Fans, by contrast, have little tolerance for it. They are voting with millions of streams against artifice in music. Songs and albums harkening back to analog instrumentation are dominating the Billboard charts, no futurism wanted.
Both A$AP Rocky, rapper and partner to Rihanna, and Grimes have taken the same position: accepting AI-generated music but not making it.

“I prefer to do things myself, practically,” A$AP Rocky told Billboard: “If somebody does a totally AI-generated song where all they did was prompt something, then I think that’s their thing. But who am I to say what’s standard and what’s not? I’m just doing me out here, and I’m doing my music practically – the right way.”
Kelly Clarkson similarly outlined her own boundary while expressing enthusiasm for AI.

Grimes, one of my own favorite musicians, has begun promoting her first new album in six years, Psy Opera, which she described to the Paris Review as capturing the “emotion of being thrust into the future”. Stereogum described the album as “AI-inspired but not AI-generated”, citing Grimes’s own insistence that her team of 70 be credited rather than reduced to machines.

Grimes offered a free license of her own voice to AI enthusiasts to make what they would three years ago. That she declined to generate her own music indicates that, even to a futurist like her, AI-generated music is lacking, similar to Rocky’s stance.
after newsletter promotion

I have also found myself listening to an AI-generated song, Bomboclat Wallahi, brought to my attention via frenetic, overstimulating videos on Instagram. Despite the song’s comical sonic maximalism, it lacks any staying power. Listening to it the day after I first heard it left no impression, similar to the way low-quality food leaves me hungry again just a few hours after eating. “Slop” is still the best word to describe AI-made content.

In contrast with artists’ nuanced stances, fans are making their position on tech-made music clear: they don’t want it. Billboard’s charts of the most popular albums and charts of the past week showcase a preference for music without obvious modification. Songs and albums that feature a simple voice-and-guitar arrangement are dominating. On the Top 200 album charts, most of the Top 10 albums foreground a singer over analog instrumentation – Olivia Rodrigo’s you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love, Ella Langley’s Dandelion, Olivia Dean’s The Art of Loving, Taylor Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl, Noah Kahan’s The Great Divide and Stick Season, and Morgan Wallen’s I’m the Problem. In the Hot 100 singles chart, the top four songs bear the same sonic signatures: Swift’s Patient Zero, Langley’s Choosin’ Texas, Stella Lefty’s Boston, Wallen’s Been by Now.

Incredibly, the Beatles’ Rubber Soul, released in 1965, also made an appearance at No 4 on last week’s Billboard rankings. Some listeners want to return to a time when producing music with artificial intelligence wasn’t even an option.

articles.title: Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks
articles.summary: Russia unilaterally frees Stephen Hubbard after US request while Steve Witkoff praises Putin as a ‘humanitarian’

blocks.text: Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington.
Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.

His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine, while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections.
Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia, rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country.
Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week.

He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”

blocks.caption: Stephen Hubbard in court in Moscow in October 2024. Photograph: Moscow city court press service/AP

blocks.text: Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a controversial deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.

The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.

Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.

Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.”
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.

blocks.caption: ‘You are a humanitarian, sir, and I salute that,’ Witkoff told Putin during their meeting. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP

blocks.text: The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo.

But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House.

During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”. Witkoff, meanwhile, said there was “some degree of momentum” behind efforts to reach a peace deal, describing the talks in Oslo as “constructive”.

Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv.
The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.

Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market.
Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes.

Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze.
