articles.title: Helen Haines has lost both legs after alleged attack but ‘her heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says
articles.summary:
Haines is in stable condition. Surgeons tried to save her right leg but both have now been amputated due to injuries

  • Get our

blocks.text: The independent MP Helen Haines has lost both legs but remains in a stable condition, two days after an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria.

Haines, the federal MP for Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg on Tuesday, but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.
Her husband, Phil Haines, provided an update on his wife’s condition at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital late on Wednesday afternoon.
Composed and clear, he said his wife had survived a “horrendous incident” and faced a long road to recovery.
“The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable,” he said.

“That is the most important thing for our family. And I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind.

“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”

Phil Haines described his wife, 65, as a fighter. The pair have been married for nearly 40 years and have three children and two grandchildren. He became emotional for a moment at the end of the statement, reflecting on his wife’s strength.
“She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover, and that is what we hope for,” he said.
“We are grateful at this stage that both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
Haines asked for donations to the charity Save the Children as his wife recovers.

Police allege Monday’s attack was targeted, and have charged Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
Nugent faced Wangaratta magistrates court earlier on Wednesday.

blocks.caption: Phil Haines and governor general Sam Mostyn speak to reporters on Wednesday afternoon. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Phil Haines was joined by the governor general, Sam Mostyn. Mostyn said she had relayed news of the incident to King Charles and praised Helen Haines’s work as a local representative, including her commitment to improving the standards of public discourse in Australia.
“This violent attack on a much loved and respected sitting member of our federal parliament must be a moment for us to pause and to choose to be better,” she said.
“We’ve got to hope that that beautiful heart, that beautiful mind will be strengthened every day by our support and our commitment to be more like Helen as part of this great democracy.”
Anthony Albanese and politicians from across federal parliament have expressed shock and anger at the alleged attack on Haines.
The incident has sparked calls for changes to politicians’ safety, with security services including the Australian federal police and Asio briefing MPs on the current landscape on Wednesday.

blocks.caption: Independent MP Helen Haines is in a stable condition. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/Reuters

blocks.text: Speaking at a vigil in Wodonga on Wednesday evening, Cathy McGowan, who held the seat of Indi before Haines, paid tribute to her friend.
“There is another level of grief, different and deeper from the actual violence, from the sorrow, the shame and the hurt,” she said.

“It’s about Helen in her role as our elected representative. In attacking her, we intuit that this is an attack on our political system, on our democracy, and especially so for all the supporters who did the democracy work getting Helen elected.”
McGowan called for the upcoming Victorian state election campaign to be conducted in a positive and constructive way. Voters go to the polls next month.
The community could not let violence win, McGowan implored.

“That we ensure the legacy of this attach on Helen will be a stronger, more vibrant and effective democracy, and from a personal perspective, all candidates and especially women, know they can run for office and be safe.”

articles.title: Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger is ‘a good idea’ as companies form deal committees
articles.summary: 'I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies,' Elon Musk says in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking

blocks.text: MUSK'S SPACEX. SpaceX's logo and an Elon Musk photo are seen in this illustration created on December 19, 2022.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
'I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies,' Elon Musk says in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking

items: Elon Musk expressed that merging SpaceX and Tesla could be beneficial, with special committees formed to explore this possibility, leading to an 8% rise in shares.

SpaceX reported a significant revenue increase driven by AI, with a net income of $4.4 billion, while its Starlink service surpassed subscriber expectations but faced declining average revenue per user.
Despite the discussions about a merger, Musk cautioned that it is premature to assume it will happen, as transaction terms have yet to be agreed upon.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Elon Musk said on Tuesday, October 20, that a merger of his two companies SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea” and that they had formed special committees to discuss a union, sending shares of the space and technology company up 8% in extended trading.

The company earlier posted its first profit as a public company and Musk said he expected annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027, as demand for its data-center space surges thanks to the AI boom.

Musk has in the past tantalized shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla, citing growing overlap between them. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting in December.

“I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” Musk said in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” which comprised independent directors, he told investors on a conference call.
The companies had formed the special committees at the request of shareholders, who ultimately would need to approve a deal, he added.

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity,” he said.

Terafab, the chip manufacturing joint venture between the two companies, should produce its first test chip around May or June of next year and aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028, Musk said on the call.

Musk added that it would be premature to assume a SpaceX-Tesla merger would happen, noting that the special committees had not agreed on transaction terms and may never do so. Tesla shares rose 1.8% in extended trading.
The world’s richest person, Musk owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, and analysts have said a merger would give him control of the combined entity.

The talks started in recent weeks and could result in SpaceX acquiring Tesla, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters, who declined to be named because they were not authorized to talk to media. Tesla has been working with an investment bank to advise on the discussions, the person said.

SpaceX’s revenue climbed 161% to $14.58 billion for the three months ended September 30 from a year earlier. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $7.56 billion, mostly from renting out data-center capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google, and Reflection AI rather than from its own models.

The third quarter offered the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI is translating into revenue, even as spending on compute infrastructure remains enormous — capital expenses nearly tripled to $19.6 billion.

The shift is reshaping a company whose financial engine has long been its Starlink internet services business and whose longer-term ambitions still hinge on getting Starship rockets into regular service. For now, though, its main business looks closer to a cloud provider’s than an AI lab’s.
SpaceX’s chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said the company expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditure in the fourth quarter.

“SpaceX delivered the quarter the bulls wanted, at least on the top line,” said Will Rhind, CEO of asset manager GraniteShares. “The story now is all about AI. The compute contracts signed earlier this year are turning into revenue faster than a lot of people thought.”
The company’s AI business spans Grok, social media platform X, and a fast-growing data-center operation. The business also turned a profit in the third quarter, compared with a year-ago loss.

SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion versus a net loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier and analysts’ expectation for a profit of $1.57 billion. On a per-share, adjusted basis, it earned 45 cents according to IBES calculations, outstripping a 13-cent average estimate.

The satellite-internet unit has continued to expand its subscriber base, aided by additional satellite launches and a growing range of consumer, enterprise, aviation, maritime and government services.

Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, above the 12.19 million analysts expected, but growth is coming at a price: average monthly revenue per subscriber has fallen from $99 in 2023 to $69 in the third quarter as it expands abroad with cheaper plans.
The company has said geographic expansion beyond the wealthiest countries could push average revenue per user lower over time.

Starship, SpaceX’s next-generation reusable rocket system, has yet to enter commercial service. It is expected to enable deployment of higher-bandwidth Starlink satellites and orbital AI-computing infrastructure. The company’s ability to turn Starship into a reliably reusable vehicle is central to its longer-term strategy.
The space segment includes commercial launches, government missions and Starship development and remains a significant source of costs and uncertainty. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger 'good idea' as companies explore union
articles.summary: Musk confirmed the long standing speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX but warned that it would be premature to assume it is happening for sure.

image.caption: Investors say a merger would create a single entity for investors who want to back Elon MuskImage: Xavier Collin/Image Press Agency/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Tech billionaire Elon Musk on Tursday said a merger between his two companies, SpaceX and Tesla, would be a "good idea" and that they had formed special committees to discuss the matter — confirming speculation of a possibly union.
"I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies," Musk said.
"Because ​I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees," which was comprised of independent directors, he told investors on a conference call.
Shares of the space tech company rose 8% in trade over Musk's comment, while Tesla's shares rose 1.8%. The space tech company had earlier posted its first profit as a public company.
About that, Musk said he expected an annual recurring revenue between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027, as demand for its data enter space surges and the AI boom.
Tesla approves $1 trillion pay deal for CEO Elon Musk
Merger not a given
This is not the first time Musk has publicly spoken about a merger between his auto-making and rocket-making companies.
Speculation about a possibly merger gained traction recently with Barclays suggesting that a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting in December.

Musk told investors that the special committees has been formed at the request of shareholders who would ultimately need to approve a deal. At least 50% of Tesla shareholders would have to approve a deal for it to go through.

"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and ​there's a lot to be ‌gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity," he said.
He added a disclaimer that it would be premature to assume a merger would happen.
Elon Musk vs. Mukesh Ambani: Battle for India’s telecom market
What investors are saying

"Going into this, I'd have said there's a 90% chance that something happens in the next two years. It's a 95% chance, I think, now. It might even be in the next year. But clearly there is momentum around this internally and I think that ‌ultimately it does happen," said Gene Munster, Managing Partner at Tesla Investor Deepwater Asset Management.
Justus Parmar, Chief Executive Officer at Frotuna Invesments said there was another benefit to the deal apart from having all of Musk's companies in one place for investors to back.

"Tesla runs a high-margin, cash-generative automotive business and there's more growth to come with the robotaxis on the way. That cash flow could help support SpaceX's bottom line and fund its very capital-intensive space exploration and launch goals, including orbital data centers," he said.
What Tesla's dramatic Roadster reveal says about Musk's strategy

articles.title: Pakistan arrests man hunted by US over $126m postage fraud case
articles.summary: Faheem Akram allegedly sold more than 5 million fake postage labels for a fixed price of $2 a piece.

blocks.text: Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.
Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.
Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.
According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.
US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.
An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.
If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

articles.title: Troubled waters: life during wartime for Iranians on the strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there

Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the…
articles.byline: Stefanie Glinski ; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz Island

blocks.text: Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.

In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.

blocks.caption: Capt Farouq pulls into the deeper waters

items: Capt Farouq pulls into the deeper waters

blocks.caption: He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home

items: He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home

blocks.text: Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.

Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.

Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.

blocks.caption: One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz

items: One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.

According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.

Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel.
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.

blocks.caption: Fishers returning from sea

items: Fishers returning from sea

blocks.caption: Two fishers carry a box at shoreline with small boat in background
Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street

items: Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street

blocks.text: Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.

blocks.caption: Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption

items: Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption

blocks.caption: Man crouched down reeling in line at water’s edge

blocks.text: Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.

blocks.caption: Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas

items: Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas

blocks.text: “This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.

Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.

blocks.caption: Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years

items: Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years

blocks.caption: Two people sit playing a board game with cafe counter behind

blocks.text: Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.

blocks.caption: Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer

items: Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer

blocks.caption: A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island

items: A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island

blocks.text: Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.

The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.

blocks.caption: Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict

items: Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict

blocks.caption: A tour guide looks out from a shaded hut over sandy terrain toward buildings and the sea
The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war

items: The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war

blocks.text: “The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.

blocks.caption: The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions

items: The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions

blocks.text: From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.

Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.

blocks.caption: One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz

items: One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.

blocks.caption: Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter

items: Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter

blocks.text: “Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”

articles.title: Rising emissions and temperatures: The cost of Trump's climate retreat is now clear
articles.summary: The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small…

image.caption: Decades of insufficient action to cut emissions mean the world will exceed 1.5 C of warming, according to the UNImage: imageBROKER/McPHOTO/BilderBox/IMAGO

blocks.text: For over a decade, scientists have warned the world must limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) to avoid the most severe consequences of climate change.
That goal is no longer within reach.

Decades of "insufficient" action on cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet means overshooting 1.5-degree temperature threshold is now "imminent and unavoidable," according to the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report.

If current climate policies continue, temperatures will rise by an average of 2.8 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within this century. But even if countries meet their new climate pledges, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6 degrees Celsius. Both scenarios would tip the world into a period of catastrophic weather extremes.

The projections reflect a gap between what governments promise to do and the action they are taking to curb emissions. Some 167 countries have submitted climate action plans to the UN, covering 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But those pledges to cut emissions fall far short of what is needed to limit warming.

Among the world's largest emitters, Indonesia, China and the United States saw emissions rise in 2025, according to preliminary estimates. The increase in the US "far exceeded that of all other countries," driven by a resurgence of coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel source — and rising electricity demand, partly linked to massive AI data center expansion.

The outlook has worsened in part because of US President Donald Trump's withdrawal of the United States from the historic Paris climate accord in which the world came together in 2015 to agree to halt climate change. The US is the second-largest annual emitter of climate-warping greenhouse gases.
Since Trump entered the Oval Office for a second time, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to climate policy, gutting environmental regulations and expanding oil and gas production.

"The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," said Bill Hare, CEO of the global science and policy institute Climate Analytics, of the report.
What does overshooting mean for the planet?

Exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius even temporarily sets humanity on a dangerous course, as it increases the risk of triggering potentially irreversible or difficult-to-undo "tipping points," like the loss of coral reefs, long-term retreat of ice sheets, and the Amazon Rainforest turning into a grassland.

As ecosystems disappear and sea levels rise, these changes could trigger a deadly chain reaction, releasing more greenhouse gases and accelerating warming, dramatically increasing the likelihood of deadly extreme weather.

This summer alone, Europe recorded more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat and nearly 1,500 people died in a flash floods in Nepal and Tibet, after climate change laid the groundwork for a glacier to collapse.

blocks.caption: Residents carry their belongings salvaged from their damaged homes filled with mud and debris following a deadly glacier collapse in NepalImage: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: But scientists maintain 1.5 degrees Celsius is not a magic number, and that every fraction of a degree of warming brings escalating risks. To reduce the risk of future damage, countries should still focus on rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels, the largest contributor to global climate change, and toward renewable energy like solar and wind.
Now the best-case scenario is overshooting 1.5 degrees Celsius for a short time before bringing temperatures back down quickly.

"Overshoot is not surrender," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a press statement. "We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees before the end of the century."
How can the world limit overshoot?

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

It would also require removing 330 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in the ground. But recent studies have cast doubt on the feasibility and costs of the technology, as well as the nascent carbon removal industry's ability to scale as quickly as required to meet climate goals.
The UN warns any delays will make the challenge harder, saying that every five years that emissions remain at current levels adds about 0.1 Celsius to projected peak warming.
"We must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 Celsius by the end of the century," Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP, said in a press release. "This is possible."
Climate policy works

Still, climate policies have proven effective in reducing emissions. The UNEP report draws on more than 200 studies that analyze how measures like carbon taxes, government climate targets, building codes and subsidies for low-carbon technologies are working.

Carbon-pricing schemes have been the most widely studied so far. China's pilot schemes reduced emissions by about 11%, while the European Union's emissions trading system saw an 8% cut, compared with projected levels without these policies.
"There are more opportunities than ever to accelerate action," according to the report, pointing to the boom in renewable energy since the adoption of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.
Pakistan's solar boom shields some from energy shocks

Global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, and solar build-out grew seven times faster. In 2024, more than 90% of renewable projects were cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives.

While total energy supply from coal, oil and gas has continued to rise, that's happened at a slower rate than was projected in 2015. And coal use is likely to peak and decline by the end of the decade.

"We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly," Andersen said. "It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies."

articles.title: ICC prosecutors drop one drug war killing from Rodrigo Duterte case
articles.summary: Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have dropped one alleged killing of a high-value drug target from their case against former president Rodrigo Duterte, after judges ruled it fell…

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 12:35pm

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on September 16, 2026, during a preparatory session as he faces charges over his “war on drugs,” which killed thousands.
AFP / Pool / Piroschka Van De Wouw

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have dropped one alleged killing of a high-value drug target from their case against former president Rodrigo Duterte, after judges ruled it fell outside the time frame of the charge, according to a court filing.

The killing, listed as Incident 57, was one of eight that prosecutors sought to add to the case ahead of trial. They filed it under Count 2, which covers the alleged murders of “high-value targets,” or suspected major drug figures, during Duterte’s first year as president, from July 2016 to July 2017.

In an October 9 ruling, Trial Chamber III said the killing fit the type and locations of crimes covered by Count 2 but took place outside that period. The judges said prosecutors could not stretch the defined period that they themselves established for the case.

The judges admitted the seven other new incidents, bringing the total to 56, up from 49 when the charges were confirmed in April. An incident can involve more than one victim: the original 49 cover 76 murders and two attempted murders. The court has not said publicly how many victims the seven new incidents add.

The filing, dated Wednesday, October 20 and signed by Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang, shows prosecutors removed Incident 57 from their trial brief, the document that lays out the case they will present in court.

Prosecutors, however, left their lists of witnesses and evidence unchanged, although the October 9 ruling had ordered those updated as well. They said material connected to the killing, combined with other evidence about it, remains relevant to “the contextual elements of crimes against humanity, and Mr Duterte’s individual criminal responsibility.” Large parts of their explanation were redacted in the public document.
A killing counts as a crime against humanity only if it was part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians carried out under a state or organizational policy.

Besides the high-value target killings, the charges cover alleged killings in Davao City while Duterte was mayor, from 2013 to around June 2016. They also cover alleged murders and attempted murders during barangay clearance operations from July 2016 to September 2018.
The trial of the former president opens November 30.

Super typhoon Rosal as of 10:40 a.m. on Oct. 21, 2026.
PAGASA / Released

MANILA, Philippines — Batanes has been placed under Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 2 as Super Typhoon Rosal (international name: Champi) maintained its strength while moving west-northwestward over the sea east of Northern Luzon, state weather bureau PAGASA said.
In its 11 a.m. bulletin, PAGASA said the center of Rosal's eye was 845 kilometers east of Northern Luzon as of 10 a.m.
The super typhoon is currently at its peak intensity, packing maximum sustained winds of 215 kilometers per hour (kph) near the center and gusts of up to 265 kph, with a central pressure of 900 hPa.
Rosal is moving west-northwestward at 25 kph while its winds extend outward up to 780 kilometers from its center.
PAGASA raised Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 2 over Batanes, warning residents of possible gale-force winds of 62 to 88 kph within 24 hours that pose minor to moderate threats to life and property.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly played Taylor Swift’s No Body, No Crime during body disposal, court told
articles.summary:
Friend of accused double murderer tells supreme court that van had lemony smell and blue tarp in back before Bunnings stop

Beau Lamarre-Condon played Taylor Swift’s song No Body, No Crime…

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon played Taylor Swift’s song No Body, No Crime while attempting to dispose of two corpses, a court has heard.
The NSW supreme court has been told he was driving to Bungonia with a friend when the song was played in the van.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

A friend of Lamarre-Condon, known to the court under the pseudonym Elizabeth Kennedy, said she thought she and the officer were going out for lunch when he picked her up on 21 February 2024 – two days after the alleged murders.
He arrived at Kennedy’s home in a white van about 3pm that day, she told the court.
Defence lawyer John Stratton SC on Wednesday suggested Lamarre-Condon told her: “I’m not joking, if you don’t want to help me I completely understand and I won’t be mad”.
He claimed Lamarre-Condon lifted a tarpaulin, which had been stored in the back of the van, and showed Baird’s deceased head.
Stratton said the officer had told her Baird was dead and suggested Kennedy said: “this is like a Taylor Swift song, No Body, No Crime” before playing the song in the car.
She denied Stratton’s suggestions and said he didn’t show her Baird’s body, nor did she choose the song.
“He was the one that put that song on in the car … it’s a very niche song,” she told the court.
“I asked him how he knew it and he said it was from the album, evermore.
“I tried to play a few more songs from the album, evermore, and he didn’t know any of them so it was very weird to me he knew that song.”
Kennedy on Wednesday morning offered her own account of events to the court.
She said she noticed a blue tarp in the back of the van and a lemony smell, like it had just been cleaned.
As Lamarre-Condon took the wheel, the drive got longer and longer, she said.
Every time she asked how much further, he would respond, “just 50 more minutes”. It ended up being a two-hour drive to Goulburn and Bungonia, about 150km away, the court heard.
The van’s windows were open the entire trip and the air-conditioning was on full blast and freezing, Kennedy told the jury.
She said that during the drive he seemed “bubbly” and talked about Swift, who was touring Australia at that time, as well as a Europe trip they were planning together.
They eventually stopped at Bunnings Goulburn, the court heard.

In a statement read to the court on Wednesday morning, a Bunnings sales assistant said he had been approached by two customers that day who claimed they were staying at a friend’s farm in nearby Bungonia and had locked themselves out.
The worker suggested they use an angle grinder.

blocks.caption: A screenshot of Beau Lamarre-Condon captured on CCTV at Bunnings Alexandria in Sydney on 20 February, 2024. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the murders, saying the men were killed in self-defence. Photograph: NSW supreme court/PR HANDOUT

blocks.text: As Lamarre-Condon and Kennedy went to the Bunnings checkout, the officer asked her to pay for an angle grinder and padlock because he did not have cash with him, she said.
The two then drove to Cella Farm in Bungonia and Lamarre-Condon explained he knew the people who owned the property.
When they arrived, he asked her to put garbage bags over the van’s number plates, but she refused, so he did it himself, Kennedy said.
He then cut the padlock off the gate, cutting himself in the process and asked Kennedy to wait there and not turn on her phone.
“He left me there and drove out of sight behind the house where the bigger dam was,” she told the court.
Kennedy began having a panic attack and, when Lamarre-Condon returned 30 or 40 minutes later, he told her to shush and asked if she had called anyone or turned on her phone.
As they began the return journey to Sydney, he asked if they could go back to Bungonia but she said she needed to be home.
Lamarre-Condon was “weird and cryptic” on the trip back, the court heard.
“It seemed like something went wrong and he wouldn’t tell me about it,” Kennedy told the court.
At one point he almost ran over a bird and said, ‘you know I’d never hurt an animal, right?’, Kennedy said.
Lamarre-Condon attempted to call another police officer friend during the drive.
When the friend didn’t pick up, he said: “‘fuck fuck fuck’ and then he sort of panicked and that’s when he started saying, ‘if I’m quiet, I’m not angry, I’m just thinking’”, the court heard.
He told Kennedy he would have to return to Bungonia and that he would be up all night.
She asked why and he said he could not tell her because he did not want to involve her, the court heard.
He then asked if she could buy him a peach Lipton ice tea as he needed caffeine but didn’t drink coffee.
As she entered the service station to purchase the beverage, he also asked her to fuel up the van, but she couldn’t do it because she didn’t know how to drive or fill up a vehicle.
He was “visibly annoyed” before he swore and jumped out of the car. When asked why he did not want to do it, Kennedy told the court he said he did not want to be on camera.
As they left, she noticed the blue tarp was no longer in the back of the van.
The bodies of Baird and Davies were later found in Bungonia.
The defence team claims Baird and Davies were accidentally shot as the accused acted in “self-defence”.
Lamarre-Condon cleaned up the scene and disposed of the bodies afterwards because he “panicked considerably”, Stratton SC has said.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Why does Elon Musk want to merge Tesla and SpaceX?
articles.summary: Musk, who is CEO of both companies, says there is "a lot to be gained" from the merger, which would be the biggest in history.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByOsmond Chia
Business reporter
Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."

The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (£1.1bn) and SpaceX at $2tn (£1.5tn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
How likely is the merger?
"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, the Chief Technology Advisor at The Futurum Group, a market research company.

The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.
The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.
Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.
Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?

But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as CEO of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.
Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.
He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.
But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.
"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.
SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 1.5%.
What would it mean for customers?
Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.
In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.
Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models.
Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the CyberTruck and Model 3

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images
Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the CyberTruck and Model 3
Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said.
"The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.
The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.
The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January.
What does Musk get out of it?
The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.
The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.
A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said.
"The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.
However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.
The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.
Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn.
"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.
The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

articles.title: Fifth foreign firm pulls out of controversial Israeli cable car project to East Jerusalem
articles.summary:
Rights groups say the planned 1.4km route, which ends at compound run by far-right settler group Elad, will displace Palestinians and reshape the cultural landscape

A fifth foreign…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem

blocks.text: A fifth foreign company has pulled out of a plan to build a cable car from West to East Jerusalem that threatens to involve the seizure of land and property rights from dozens of Palestinian families along its route, but local authorities insist the scheme is proceeding as planned.

The project appeared to have stalled for four years until late September, just weeks before Israel’s 27 October elections, when the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA) issued a notice of intent to award a contract without a public tender to ROPES, a cable car engineering consultancy based in South Tyrol, Italy.
However, Stephan Obexer, chief executive of ROPES told the Guardian his company had declined the consultancy work because of another commitment in India.

The 1.4km cable car route, approved by the Israeli government in 2019 and upheld by the high court in 2022, would connect West Jerusalem to a planned 16,000 sq metres tourist complex promoted by Elad, a settler organisation seeking to consolidate Israeli control over Palestinian areas of occupied East Jerusalem.

The Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territories began in 1967 and the Old City and the rest of the eastern half of Jerusalem were fully annexed in 1980, although they are still considered occupied under international law.

According to Emek Shaveh, an Israeli NGO, the JDA had recently accelerated plans for a long-delayed cable car through occupied East Jerusalem, where Israel’s continued presence has been ruled unlawful by the international court of justice, in a project once described by former Jerusalem mayor Nir Barkat as a way for visitors to “understand who is truly the landlord of the city”.

‘‘This project threatens the Palestinian communities and the timeless landscape of Jerusalem’s historic core,’’ said Emek Shaveh in a recent statement. ‘‘It is clear that the project’s central motivation is to consolidate the settlers’ hold in those areas as part of an effort to displace Palestinians from the Historic Basin and reshape Jerusalem’s cultural landscape.’’
The plan comes amid escalating settler violence and efforts to seize Palestinian land across the occupied territories.

At least four foreign companies – three French and one Swiss – have expressed interest in the project, but several have withdrawn over its political sensitivity, according to Haaretz, an Israeli newspaper. In 2015, the French government urged one company not to participate. Another French company, CNA, pulled out less than a year ago, followed more recently by Switzerland’s Histec Engineering.
ROPES did not respond to a request for a written statement or questions about whether legal concerns over the project’s location in occupied East Jerusalem had influenced its decision.
The JDA did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

But a spokesperson for the JDA told Haaretz: “Following the high court of justice’s dismissal of petitions against the project about a year and a half ago, the cable car continues to proceed according to plan and in accordance with the timetables set. Steps to promote the project are subject to the mandatory tenders law, and the tender is expected to be ready for publication in the coming months once its formulation is completed.”

The move has sparked protests from Israeli heritage and environmental groups and Palestinians in Silwan, an East Jerusalem neighbourhood at the foot of the Old City, who warn that the project threatens Palestinian heritage in territory they seek for a future state and would see cable cars passing just metres above their homes.

“The cable car stands in complete contradiction to the historic principle that no large buildings or infrastructure should be built around the Old City,’’ says Alon Arad, an archaeologist and the executive director of Emek Shaveh. ‘‘It is particularly troubling that the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, the body responsible for upholding this principle, is cooperating with the project.

“To understand the political context, one must look at the route: it begins in West Jerusalem and ends at a compound run by the far-right settler organisation Elad Foundation, which stands to benefit from a project costing the state around half a billion shekels. Elad is notorious for using state resources to advance its political agenda in East Jerusalem, taking over Palestinian properties, evicting families and settling Jewish residents in their place.”
The Elad Foundation, which does not appear to be formally involved in the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

blocks.caption: Palestinian women shopping for bread in the Old City of Jerusalem during Ramadan.  Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to rights groups, the cable car project directly threatens about 54 Palestinian homes along its route in the Wadi Hilweh neighbourhood in Silwan, with the expropriation of either land or air rights, and indirectly threatens many others in the vicinity. Israeli authorities have issued 17 expropriation notices covering about 8.7 dunams (2.15 acres) of land along the proposed route, where pylons supporting the cable car would be erected.

“These buildings, home to roughly 450 residents, lie directly beneath the proposed route,” said Sari Kronish, an architect and director of the East Jerusalem department at Bimkom, an Israeli planning rights organisation. “Cable cars would pass as close as four metres above rooftops and near residential windows, violating residents’ privacy and restricting future development. Expropriations of land and homes for support pillars have already been set in motion, leaving residents in a constant state of uncertainty.”
Reached by the Guardian, the Israel Nature and Parks Authority said: “Our involvement was limited to providing feedback on the proposed alternatives.”

Across occupied East Jerusalem, Israeli settlers are increasingly taking over Palestinian properties, while authorities have stepped up demolitions of homes lacking building permits, displacing families. The Mount of Olives, home to some of Christianity’s holiest sites, has also become a target of settler expansion, raising concerns among churches that own land there.

The campaign has intensified since the war in Gaza started in October 2023 amid accelerating land seizures and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank, where more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers.

blocks.caption: The surge in settler violence includes this week’s attack on European diplomats. Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Settler violence has surged during the annual olive harvest. On 16 October, settlers attacked Palestinian villages, burning cars and trees and injuring a Washington Post photographer. The following day, settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinian olive pickers, injuring three people and damaging a diplomatic vehicle.

articles.title: 'Trash Island' or DC landmark? How a golf course got Trump in a messy legal dispute
articles.summary: Trump said he has plans to turn a 106-year-old public golf course in Washington DC into a tournament-capable golf course for pros, but local golfers are not happy.

blocks.text: For Jourdain Yardan, golfing at the East Potomac Golf Links on Washington DC's waterfront is a twice-weekly ritual.

"Anyone from any walk of life, whether they're starting to play golf or whether they're a ... seasoned golfer, they can come out here and play golf at a pretty reasonable rate," the 35-year-old told the BBC while putting on the course on Monday.
But President Donald Trump does not seem convinced of its charms, calling the 106-year-old course "Trash Island" Monday evening on Truth Social.

Now, he intends to shut it down for renovations to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments".

The renovation is part of the president's sprawling and controversial efforts to shape the US capital, which include a new White House ballroom, a 250-foot-tall arch and other changes to longstanding landmarks. The golf course is a smaller project, but deeply personal to many who live in the city.
Yardan described a potential shuttering, even if temporary, as a "huge dent" in DC culture that could change the heart of the space.
Trump, an avid golfer and owner of more than a dozen courses, says his vision for the course will make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World".
But courts will need to mediate the dispute between the White House and the community before Trump can realize his plans.

The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital. A lawsuit from the DC Preservation League and two golfers from the course asks the court to stop Trump's planned renovation.
"Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves," Democracy Forward, the group representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement on social media.
The legal fight intensified this month after the government began large-scale tree removal on the course without giving the court or plaintiffs notice.
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to stop its redevelopment plans until at least 26 October.

Despite the work stoppage, Trump took to social media on Sunday to announce that the course will be closed for 15-months beginning in November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.

"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," Trump wrote in his post on Sunday.
While golfer Thomas Snow, who is not part of the suit, conceded the course could use a "facelift", he thinks the president's description of the course is a "gross overstatement".

Currently, East Potomac does not offer the manicured experience one might find at the luxury, private golf courses the president is known for building. The public course is open to all and does not require a membership to access.
The facilities at the DC course are more modest, offering food court-style dining rather than amenities such as white tablecloth restaurants and upscale locker rooms.
Golfers like Snow and Yardan who regularly play the courses at East Potomac, told the BBC it offers a rare combination of affordability and proximity to the city.
"You start to clear everything out and it just starts to become an empty plot of land that you just hit golf balls on; I think it gets rid of the culture of the golf course," Yardan said.
As a 70-year-old golfer, Snow pays $29 (£21.65) for 18 holes when he visits East Potomac.
"There's no place in the whole DMV (the metropolitan region including DC and its Maryland and Virginia suburbs) that you can play a nice 18 holes for that price point," he said.
Snow worries that if Trump's proposal moves forward, people will be priced out.
Yardan, the twice-weekly golfer, echoed those concerns.
"Anytime you hear about big league, big golfers, that also includes big prices," he said. "The biggest thing that I like about this golf course .. is that it's affordable," he said.

articles.title: Pangilinan to Marcos: You sent Duterte and Romualdez to jail, you can expel China’s envoy
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. continues to face pressure from lawmakers to expel China’s ambassador, this time from Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, who reminded him that his government was able to put…

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 11:19am
President Marcos accepts the credentials of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan at Malacañang last December. Looking on is Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro.
Presidential Communications Office

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. continues to face pressure from lawmakers to expel China’s ambassador, this time from Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, who reminded him that his government was able to put former President Rodrigo Duterte and his own cousin behind bars.
In a strongly worded statement Tuesday night, Pangilinan challenged the president to take action on the Chinese ambassador.

"Mr. President, if you can send Duterte, Quiboloy and Romualdez to jail, declare POGO illegal and have them shutdown, assert our sovereignty against Chinese aggression then you can most certainly send this arrogant, insulting, crude and insolent alien back to his country of origin," Pangilinan said.
"I have witnessed and thus know that you have what it takes, Mr President. But if you don't use it, you lose it," he said, calling Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan a "hooligan" who should be sent home.

This is Pangilinan's third swipe at the diplomat in days, having previously said the ambassador can "easily leave Manila and go back to China." On Monday, Pangilinan suggested Chinese diplomats who stray from the Communist Party line risk harsh punishment at home.

In the Senate, at least two resolutions have been filed urging the executive branch to consider declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata or seek his expulsion. About 10 members of the House of Representatives have separately urged the president to expel Jing, who they say has "clearly overstayed his welcome."

But the Palace itself has been cool to these calls. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said on Monday that Marcos would not want to have such a declaration for any foreign envoy in the country, though she stressed the Palace respected lawmakers' views.
The DFA has described a persona non grata declaration as a last resort that carries high diplomatic and reciprocal costs.

Neither the Senate nor the House has the power to declare a foreign diplomat persona non grata. This is a power that's only with the executive, specifically the president and the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA). A sending state however can also recall a diplomat and end their functions.

Jing, after meeting Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro on Monday, released a statement through the Chinese Embassy, saying he has been taken out of context. He accused the Philippine side of committing "smear and slander" against Beijing.

The dispute began on October 15, when Jing, speaking to reporters after a forum in Quezon City, said China would prevail in any armed confrontation but had chosen restraint. "If we want to use force, we may easily win," he said, adding that Manila should count itself lucky to have China as a neighbor.

The DFA answered the same day with a rare public rebuke, saying the remark conveyed a "thinly veiled threat of the use of force." Marcos said the next day it "sounds very much to me like a threat" and that he wanted to hear from Jing what he meant.

articles.title: Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of Starlink in Ukraine — report
articles.summary: Elon Musk "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network," the Wall Street Journal reported.

image.caption: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of restricting Starlink service in the country [FILE: May 30, 2025]Image: Nathan Howard/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tech billionaire Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US officials.
Kyiv uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the service means restricting the country's attack and defense missions against Russia.

Last week, Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, the report said citing unnamed sources. The move rendered some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless, it added.
Two people told the Journal that Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call, soon after the slowdown became public.

Some US officials, the report said, believed Musk acted unilaterally and that Trump did not specifically order retribution against Ukraine. However, one person familiar with the situation said Musk talked to multiple senior administration officials, including Trump, even before imposing the speed limitation.
Both Musk and Trump have expressed anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices.
The report also comes after Trump's comments last week that he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access.
Musk had said that any limits on speed or use were decided by the US military or the president.
Musk, SpaceX, and the White House are yet to respond to the report.

articles.title: SC declares provisions of 2024, 2025, 2026 national budgets unconstitutional
articles.summary: The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional key provisions of the 2024, 2025, and 2026 General Appropriations Acts (GAA) over unauthorized congressional increases to unprogrammed standby funds and…

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 10:51am

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional key provisions of the 2024, 2025, and 2026 General Appropriations Acts (GAA) over unauthorized congressional increases to unprogrammed standby funds and specific special accounts.

In a decision penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and released on October 7, the high court’s En Banc declared Republic Act No. 11975, or the 2024 GAA, unconstitutional after Congress increased unprogrammed appropriations by P449.5 billion.
The ruling also granted the petition filed by the late lawmaker Edcel Lagman and several others and partly granted the petition of former Sen. Aquilino Pimentel III.

The high court likewise granted the petition filed by the Filipinos for Peace, Justice and Progress Movement, Inc. et al., declaring RA 12116, or the 2025 GAA, unconstitutional due to a P17.99-billion increase made by lawmakers to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Special Road Fund.

Additionally, the high court found that a P12.75-billion increase in Special Accounts in the General Fund (SAGF) across certain agencies violated the Administrative Code, which bars Congress from inflating special provision amounts beyond the President’s original proposal.

Acting on a petition by lawmakers Edgar Erice and Leila De Lima, the Court also voided Special Provisions 1(a) and (b), Chapter XLIII of the 2026 GAA, issuing a permanent injunction against the Senate, House of Representatives, Office of the Executive Secretary, and Department of Budget and Management from implementing them.

The Supreme Court explained that unprogrammed appropriations, which are contingent or standby authorizations released only when excess revenues or non-tax funds materialize, are not unconstitutional per se.

According to the high court, such standby funds become invalid when they lack clear standards, as this effectively gives the Executive unchecked spending power, compromises funding for programmed projects when revenue projections fall short, and violates the constitutional budget ceiling under Article VI, Section 25(1), which applies to combined programmed and unprogrammed allocations.
What was struck down
The High Court ruled that the 2024 General Appropriations Act was unconstitutional because Congress, through the Bicameral Conference Committee, bloated unprogrammed allocations by P449.5 billion.
This massive upward adjustment raised the unprogrammed budget from the President's proposed P281.9 billion in the National Expenditure Program to P731.4 billion in the final law.

The high court explained that the constitutional prohibition against Congress increasing the President's recommended budget applies to the total sum of both programmed and unprogrammed appropriations.
By leaving the programmed budget unchanged while heavily inflating unprogrammed items, Congress effectively bypassed the Executive's spending ceiling.

“The purpose of Article VI, Section 25(1) of the Constitution, which prohibits Congress from increasing the appropriations recommended by the president, is to maintain fiscal discipline and prevent excessive public expenditures that could balloon the budget deficit. This constitutional limit requires that the national budget be anchored on the Executive's projections of revenues and expenditures and on a coherent fiscal plan based on actual economic realities,” the Supreme Court said.
The decision also struck down the "Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs," popularly known as SAGIP, which was included in the 2024 and 2025 budgets.
The high court classified SAGIP as a prohibited lump-sum appropriation that gave the Executive unchecked post-enactment discretion to identify projects and allocate funds.

According to the Supreme Court, this mechanism allowed the Executive to act as a legislative authority after the budget had already passed, subverting the constitutional process of presentment and impairing the President's item-veto power.

“SAGIP is similarly unconstitutional because it is a prohibited lump sum appropriation, as defined in Belgica v Ochoa. It provides a singular lump sum amount as a source of funding for multiple purposes,” the Supreme Court said.

“Through the SAGIP lump sum appropriation, the Executive had increased latitude to determine spending priorities after the budget has been enacted. There is weakened transparency and accountability because the specific projects are itemized only during the execution stage, without the benefit of public discussion and oversight. This effectively diluted Congress's control over public spending in contravention of Constitutional safeguards,” it added.
Furthermore, under the 2025 General Appropriations Act, the Supreme Court declared the P17.992-billion increase in the programmed line-item appropriation for the Special Road Fund unconstitutional.
The fund, sourced from Motor Vehicle User's Charge collections, is a statutorily earmarked Special Account in the General Fund.

The high court ruled that while Congress generally has the discretion to supplement such funds, the Administrative Code explicitly prohibits the legislature from increasing the amounts specified in special provisions beyond what is proposed by the President.

For the 2026 General Appropriations Act, the Court nullified Special Provisions 1(a) and 1(b) under Chapter XLIII, which authorized the use of unprogrammed funds based on excess collections from individual non-tax revenue sources or new revenue streams.

The high court reaffirmed its previous doctrine that unprogrammed funds can only be triggered when aggregate revenue collections exceed the total revenue targets assumed in the Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing.

According to the Supreme Court, pegging triggers to individual or isolated revenue sources creates an "artificial surplus" that disregards the overall budget plan, fosters deficits, and violates the Constitution.

“Furthermore, from a genuine surplus originally contemplated to fund the unprogrammed appropriations, the fiscal triggers morphed into an artificial surplus brought about by a change in the reckoning of excess revenues from total/holistic view to individual revenue targets,” the Supreme Court said.

Consequently, the Senate, the House of Representatives, the Office of the Executive Secretary, and the Department of Budget and Management have been permanently prohibited from implementing these specific provisions of the 2026 GAA.

While the Court applied the doctrine of operative fact to protect the programs, projects, and good-faith beneficiaries who had already relied on the 2024 and 2025 budgets, it explicitly excluded the authors, proponents, and implementors of the unconstitutional provisions from this protection.
The ruling leaves these public officials open to potential civil, criminal, and administrative liabilities unless they can prove before the proper tribunals that they acted in good faith.

“However, this protection does not extend to the authors, proponents, and implementors of the aforementioned laws. These officials remain subject to criminal, civil, and administrative liability unless the proper tribunals explicitly find that they acted in good faith,” the Supreme Court said.

articles.title: Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again
articles.summary: The president thrust Springfield, Ohio, into the spotlight with a false pet-eating claim - years later, it remains at the heart of the immigration debate.

blocks.text: Springfield, in south-west Ohio, was thrust into the spotlight in 2024 when Trump repeated a false claim about Haitian immigrants eating pets
ByTom Bateman
reporting from Ohio

In this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it.

To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back".

But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country.
This story contains some distressing details
Pierre Damas Bel, 20, arrived in Springfield to join his father and stepmother in 2024.

He fled his native Haiti, which was gripped by political instability and gang warfare. He entered the US with the government's permission under a now-defunct Biden-era programme for migrants waiting in Mexico.
Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States.
TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country.
Bel aspired to build a life in America, the friend said. He was an honours student, talented athlete and cadet in a high school programme training students to become officers in the US Armed Forces.
But in June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pierre Damas Bel's family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear an ankle monitor

blocks.text: Pierre Damas Bel's family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear an ankle monitor
Bel was told to report to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office where he was fitted with an ankle monitor which is used to track migrants facing deportation.

He wrote on Instagram that he felt "shame and humiliation" at having to wear the tag. And on 31 August, he parked his car on the side of a highway near Springfield, walked into oncoming traffic and was killed.
His family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear the ankle monitor.
The Department for Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to questions from the BBC about Bel's case. ICE has previously rejected "any attempt to blame ICE for the death".

"Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," a spokesperson told US media earlier this year when asked about the case.
In the weeks before his death, Bel attended a Springfield support centre for Haitians facing deportation.
Its co-founder, Viles Dorsainvil, told the BBC that Bel had been in the process of filing a motion asking ICE to remove the tag.
"He went twice to the ICE facilities… begging them to remove the ankle monitor," he said. "He did everything right to be here until they put the tag on him."
In total, more than a million immigrants from 13 countries have had TPS terminated by the Trump administration. The changes meant many went from being legal to unauthorised migrants overnight.

In 2024, Trump made securing the border and the mass deportation of undocumented migrants core pledges in his election campaign. Polls suggest the border policy continues to have strong support among Republicans, but the nature of his immigration enforcement campaign has seen a drop in backing this year.
Watch: How Trump's mass deportation drive is playing out in Ohio

Ohio has become a swing state in the coming midterm Congressional elections, and one of two Republican-held Senate seats is up for grabs. Trump has visited the state twice already in an attempt to rally turnout and counter a slide in his approval ratings.
At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, earlier this month, Trump returned to the topic of Springfield.

"You have a little town, beautiful little town in Ohio where they dropped about 35,000 Haitians. Well, they're being taken out and they're almost going to be gone and we're giving their town back," he said to cheers.

The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in its favour in the summer.

"The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty," James Percival, the general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said after the court's ruling. "This is a win for the rule of law and common sense."

In a social media post in August, the Department of Homeland Security posted a video of Haitians in chains wearing white uniforms being led onto a deportation flight. The video, accompanied by jaunty music, told Haitians whose TPS had expired to "LEAVE IMMEDIATELY".
The Trump administration has said it is conducting law enforcement operations in the town to keep Americans safe. It has also argued that Haiti is safe enough to return to.
The country is subject to the US State Department's highest Level 4 "Do Not Travel" danger warning.
