A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.

Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.

Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
"I think we will have good results too," he said.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

articles.title: Lawsuit challenging Trump's tariffs against Canada filed in U.S. Court of International Trade
articles.summary: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.

image.caption: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada was filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade Tuesday. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.
Case was filed by the Liberty Justice Center on behalf of a U.S. business
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 20, 2026 3:59 PM EDT | Last Updated: 16 minutes ago

The lawsuit, filed Tuesday by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of U.S. food importer Gellert Global Group, argues Trump's use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president.

"Using the Section 338, which is, in my opinion, a dormant statute from 1930 that has never been used before, just said to us that this is wrong and we should do something about it," Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht said in an interview from Chicago with CBC's Katie Simpson.
Trump used Section 338 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August.
The same statute was used the following month to ban the import of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.
Lawsuit argues Canadian policies don't justify tariffs

The White House has said Section 338 empowers the president to impose tariffs when a country puts U.S. exporters at a disadvantage relative to exporters in other countries — even though the law has never been used for that purpose.
U.S. officials have said the latest duties are a response to provincial bans on U.S. liquor, Canada's supply managed dairy system and quotas on certain U.S. vehicles.
Tuesday's lawsuit said the Canadian policies don't justify the sweeping tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.

items: Trump says 'very bad' Canada is being 'taught a little lesson' as trade action escalates
Fact-checking the White House statement of facts about Canada

blocks.text: It notes two of the measures — auto quotas and liquor bans — were actually a response to Trump's own tariff measures.

The lawsuit also said Canada's dairy supply management involves policies agreed to under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as CUSMA, which was negotiated during the first Trump administration.

"This has real world consequences on not just the importers but the consumers in both countries," Albrecht said. "And I think it has even broader implications given the nature of the two countries and our historical relationship to each other."
She said she accepts that tariffs are one of Trump's signature policies, but says the way they are being implemented in this case is wrong.
"He has always been in love with tariffs, in my opinion, primarily because it's revenue … I can respect that," Albrecht said. "But in this case, it's wrong and it's violating our Constitution."
Feds have hired 'best lawyers' to advise on Stelco next steps, says Joly

A Trump administration official, commenting on background, said the president's actions will be vigorously defended in court. The official said Tuesday's lawsuit won't deter the president's commitment to levelling the playing field for American workers, farmers and firms.
Concerns beyond Canada
But in the meantime, the Trump administration's actions are leading to consequences for American businesses.

Thomas Gellert, co-chief executive officer of Gellert Global Group, said the company has "spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry."
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," Gellert said in the news release.

The company is being hit by the trade war on all sides, it goes on to say. It pays a 50 per cent tariff on imports of Canadian cheese but is also slammed by Ottawa's retaliatory tariffs on the American-made cheeses that its Canadian division sells in Canada.

The company cites the experience of one of its Canadian cheese suppliers to show how the integrated North American market is being disrupted by the tariff dispute. It gets milk from dairy farmers in Upstate New York, which is processed into brie in Canada, which is then sent back to the United States.
"The tariffs hit American farmers and businesses on both sides of that transaction," the news release said.

The case raises concerns beyond Canada, the news release said. If the duties remain unchecked, any president could use Section 338 to impose tariffs and trade restrictions without meaningful congressional control.
The lawsuit asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful and order a refund.

The Liberty Justice Center was previously involved in the legal challenge against Trump's use of the International Economic Emergency Powers Act of 1977 for the so-called "Liberation Day" and fentanyl-related tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.
In February, America's top court concluded it was not legal for Trump to use the statute, known as IEEPA, because the U.S. Constitution very clearly gives Congress power over taxes and tariffs.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Kelly Geraldine Malone is a reporter for The Canadian Press.
With files from CBC's Katie Simpson

articles.title: Zelenskyy visits Norway amid Trump White House tensions
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy met with Norwegian and Finnish leaders in Oslo and held talks with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Trump is pressuring Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with…

image.caption: Zelenskyy hugged US envoy Steve Witkoff at the meeting with Finnish and Norwegian leaders looking on Image: Heiko Junge/NTB/AFP

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Norway on Tuesday as Ukraine faces renewed tension in its relationship with US President Donald Trump and his administration.
Finland's Stubb: 'Today was a good day for peace'

During the visit, Zelenskyy met with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo, along with Trump envoy Steve Witkoff. The US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the meeting remotely.
Store described the meeting involving the European and the US sides as "good and constructive" at a press conference.
"US and European teams have done substantive work on key issues together with Ukraine," Store said.
Stubb said, "Today was a good day for peace." The Finnish president said Witkoff intends to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders and discuss ideas from the Oslo meeting.

blocks.caption: Trump envoy Steve Witkoff was not present at the press conference after the meeting Image: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP

blocks.text: The Oslo meeting comes as Zelenskyy has accused the US of withholding intelligence from Ukraine in advance of Russian strikes and delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles.
Zelenskyy: Early intel warnings from partners on Russian strikes resume
Zelenskyy said he held a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier in the day and said Ukraine is now receiving early warnings from its partners ahead of Russian strikes.

"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said of the Russian-launched missiles while standing next to Finnish and Norwegian leaders.
There are also media reports that Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a meeting to possibly discuss Ukraine and other issues.

"I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them," Zelenskyy said, but added that if Ukraine is discussed, it would be acceptable only if Ukrainians are at the negotiating table.
Trump ramps up attacks on Zelenskyy as US midterms loom

Earlier this month, Zelenskyy criticized a deal struck between the Trump administration and Russia to buy Russian diesel fuel. Oil and gas export revenues are vital for the Russian economy and war efforts in Ukraine.
How Trump is helping Putin

Trump has criticized Zelenskyy and blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for high diesel prices. Prices have increased dramatically since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to US attacks.

Zelenskyy on Tuesday said he is supportive of Trump's suggestion to stop attacks on energy sites, with Russia also doing the same in regard to Ukraine as part of an "energy ceasefire." However, Zelenskyy said Russia is unwilling to stop its attacks on Ukraine.
At a recent European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy smiled at the suggestion that he is being made a scapegoat by Trump.

The US president is looking for someone else to blame for high domestic energy costs ahead of midterm congressional elections onb November 3. If the opposition Democrats take back control of the US House and Senate, it could constrain Trump's powers in his last two years in office.
In comments to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, Trump said he wants Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia and suggested Moscow has the upper hand.

Ukraine has been fighting off a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022. In the past, Trump has blamed Zelenskyy for the war and on Tuesday again said it was up to Kyiv to end the Russian invasion.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
Trump said he also spoke with Putin about Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher detained in Russia accused of acting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces.
"I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said.

articles.title: Helen Haines live updates: Alleged attacker Brendan Nugent to face court in Wangaratta this morning
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live.

  • Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn…

blocks.text: Tracee Hutchison will not run in Victoria’s state election in November, despite winning almost a quarter of first preferences at the by-election in May, citing rising violence towards women.
Speaking to AAP, Hutchison shared her distress for Helen Haines and also recalled her personal experience of “a sustained, organised harassment and bullying campaign”.
double quotation markThe verbal harassment I experienced, and that the women my team did, was unlike anything I had anticipated.
Hutchison said she reported threats and feeling unsafe to the Victorian Electoral Commission every day during pre-polling.
double quotation markThere is no framework for the officers to do anything other than come out to the polling booth and tell everyone to behave. They then go back inside and people kick off again.

Helen Haines’ alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.

blocks.caption: Brendan Nugent will appear in court this morning to face three charges after the alleged attack. Photograph: Australian Broadcasting Corporation/Reuters

blocks.text: He was held overnight to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court this morning at 9.30am, Victoria police confirmed in a statement, adding that it would be alleged the attack was targeted.
Read the full story here:
We’ll have all the developments as they happen.
Good morning and welcome to our rolling coverage of the attack on Helen Haines.

A man will appear at Wangaratta court at 9.30am this morning charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
Before that, Victoria’s police chief Mike Bush and AFP commissioner Krissy Barrett will give a press conference in Melbourne at 9am to give a briefing about the investigation.
We’ll have all the latest developments.

articles.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
articles.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.
The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.
The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
The White House has been contacted for comment.

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.
Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.
The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".
The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.
Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.
"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.
The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.
"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.
The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.

It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.

Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

articles.title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau
articles.summary:
Police seized dozens of hepatitis B vaccines from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns

Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy…

blocks.text: Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.

The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.

The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.
Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.
“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.

The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.

Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.

Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.
The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.

The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.

“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”

The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.

“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.

articles.title: Cornell Jane Doe says embattled university head doubted her gang-rape allegation
articles.summary: As a no-confidence vote looms, Cornell says the characterisation of the head's reaction is "incorrect".

blocks.text: In a two-page letter dated 14 October and obtained by the BBC, Doe told the faculty senate that after she reported the alleged rape, she received "a second-hand account" of Kotlikoff's reaction and that his "initial response" was "along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'"
Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on 8 November, about three weeks after the fraternity party.

She noted that Kotlikoff had a conversation with the then-president of her sorority and that other staff members were present, at least one of whom "appeared distressed" by the college president's question.

Doe said in her letter: "It diminished my confidence in the administration's ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school."
She said she wrote the letter so that faculty "can make an informed choice" ahead of their 28 October vote on whether to express no confidence in Kotlikoff's leadership.
The university confirmed receipt of the letter from Doe's lawyer.

But in a statement to the BBC, a Cornell spokesperson said: "The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account."

The spokesperson said Kotlikoff's question about the delay in reporting the alleged rape "was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell's anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024".
"He was not questioning Jane Doe's reporting," the spokesperson said.
Kotlikoff, who has led the Ithaca-based institution for 26 years, was grilled by the faculty senate last Wednesday.
Staff said they were "deeply disturbed" by his handling of the case and accused him of lacking an "emotional response", according to recordings obtained by the BBC.
Kotlikoff highlighted changes the university had introduced as a result of Doe's allegations, including banning fraternity parties.
"We are all extraordinarily upset by the events at Cornell in October of 2024," he said.
The faculty senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff at Cornell, scheduled their no-confidence vote for 28 October.
In recordings of the meeting, faculty said sexual misconduct on campus was a systemic problem that demanded "systemic attention".
Paul Ortiz, a labour history professor who sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said students had told faculty they "feel unsafe walking to the library after dark".
He accused Cornell of treating rape "as more of a 'PR problem' than a heinous crime".

articles.title: Nigeria records its first Ebola case, in capital Abuja
articles.summary: Nigeria has reported its first known case of Ebola during Africa's latest outbreak originating in the DRC. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the patient was a woman who had recently flown to…

image.caption: The vast majority of the known Ebola cases in the outbreak are still located in the Democratic Republic of Congo, but the number of affected countries is rising [FILE: October 19, 2026]Image: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nigeria's Health Ministry on Tuesday confirmed that the country had recorded its first known case of Ebola in the current outbreak. A woman who recently arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

The outbreak is thought to have started in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, not far from the Ugandan border, with Uganda the second country to record infections. It also recently spread to Kenya in limited numbers, with nine known cases recorded this month.
The overwhelming majority of known cases, however, remain confined to the DRC, particularly its eastern provinces.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak
What do we know about the Nigerian case of Ebola?
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said that the patient was a woman who had "recently arrived on an international flight from Uganda."

She first began to exhibit symptoms on October 7, and was admitted to a private Abuja hospital on October 11, before being tested and diagnosed with Ebola. He said authorities had already begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient.
"We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all contacts the individual may have had," he said.

Nigeria's Center for Disease Control said two weeks ago that it was stepping up surveillance after the first recorded cases in Kenya, saying it was improving the country's preparedness for a possible outbreak.

"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of healthcare workers," the agency said.
Nigeria created an Ebola task force in June.

"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."

blocks.caption: Kenya has also been put on alert this month after identifying a cluster of nine cases, which officials believe all revolve around one initial patientImage: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Over 9,000 cases in current outbreak, the fastest-growing on record
While Ebola does not spread as readily as highly contagious viruses like the flu or COVID, it is considerably more dangerous to those who do contract it.
The current outbreak, involving a lesser-known strain, the Bundibugyo Ebolavirus, has led to more than 9,000 confirmed cases and more than 4,300 deaths, a fatality rate of almost 50%.

Almost all the cases and deaths are confined to the DRC, even as more countries become involved. The first patient in Kenya died, and authorities believe the other eight known cases are all part of a cluster beginning with him. They say there's no sign of a spread beyond his contacts.

Uganda, which borders the Ituri province outbreak epicenter in DRC, reported 20 cases and two deaths quite much earlier this year. It was then declared Ebola-free in late August by the World Health Organization after reaching 42 days since a confirmed case. Tuesday's case in Nigeria could potentially put this status back into question, given the Health Ministry's comments on the patient's travel history.
This year's outbreak is already the second-largest on record and by far the fastest-spreading — although modestly improved testing and diagnostic capacity may also contribute to the higher numbers.

The West African Ebola epidemic of 2014-16 led to around 11,300 deaths from around 28,500 cases — but that was over a span of around 30 months. This outbreak was first declared in May of this year, although researchers believe it likely began in small numbers of cases several months earlier.
Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew?

articles.title: As Christina Applegate reveals MS misdiagnosis, doctor warns of wrong treatment risks
articles.summary: After five years of tireless advocacy for those who shared her diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Christina Applegate has revealed that doctors now believe she was misdiagnosed.

image.caption: Christina Applegate, seen here in January 2020, says her doctors have found that she was misdiagnosed when told she had multiple sclerosis in 2021. (Jordan Strauss/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: After five years of tireless advocacy for those who shared her diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS), Christina Applegate has revealed that doctors now believe she was misdiagnosed.
"To me it comes as, like, I'm back at square one," she said of the news.

Applegate shared the story in a two-part Tuesday episode of the podcast MeSsy, which she co-hosts with Jamie-Lynn Sigler, who has MS. She had spent some months away from the show, which she explained was partially to process the revelation.
Audibly emotional at times, Applegate said that while her doctor had congratulated her when revealing she didn’t have MS, she didn't feel happy — only lost.
"You don't get misdiagnosed and all of a sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better … if anything, I've gotten worse, in some ways," she said.
"My legs aren't working, you know, all the same stuff is happening to me."

Multiple sclerosis is a complex autoimmune disease of the central nervous system. With MS, the immune system mistakenly attacks the myelin, part of the central nervous system that serves as a protective coating for the nerves. This inhibits the brain and the body from sharing information, resulting in symptoms including numbness, memory issues, fatigue, mobility issues, and sometimes vision loss.
Applegate arrives for the 29th Screen Actors Guild Awards in Century City, Calif., in February 2023. (Valerine Macon/AFP via Getty Images)
Dr. Mark Freedman, director of the multiple sclerosis research unit at The Ottawa Hospital, compared it to when the outer rubber part of a wire wears off, exposing the copper inside.

"You've now got a bare wire, which doesn't conduct well," he told CBC News. The nerve is also then more exposed to inflammation in the body, which "can then go after that little wire and cut it and destroy it all together, and then you've lost the connection permanently."
The disease takes many forms, with some patients experiencing periods of remission and relapse, and others dealing with more consistent progression causing increasing disability.

Misdiagnosis is not uncommon globally — one U.S. study from 2019 by researchers at Cedars-Sinai found that the rate of misdiagnosis was nearly one in five patients. A 2024 review looked at studies reporting misdiagnosis rates ranging from five to 41 per cent, and found an estimate of 15 per cent misdiagnosis rate when they pooled six studies.
'Tested for everything'

Applegate first announced she had MS on social media in August 2021, but it started earlier that year, she said in Tuesday's podcast episode, when she began to experience numbness in her feet, which slowly moved up her legs.
"And then the pain started," she said. "All that time, I was being tested for everything under the sun."

items: Man who lost legs to MS warming heads and hearts by knitting tuques on custom-made cot
Mom's multiple sclerosis journey an inspiration for Vancouver Goldeneyes goalie
The subject of Lyme disease is littered with misinformation. Celebrities are part of the problem, experts say

blocks.text: She said she underwent spinal MRIs, brain MRIs and a spinal tap, and that doctors thought she might have a low-grade version of the disease at first. But her symptoms kept getting worse. When doctors found nearly 40 lesions on her brain, she was officially diagnosed with MS.
"I felt like, 'OK, I have an answer,'" she said in the podcast episode.
Applegate attends the 26th Annual Screen Actors Guild Awards in Los Angeles in January 2020. (Mike Coppola/Getty Images for Turner)

But a couple years ago, her doctor paused her infusion treatments to see how her B cells would respond. When their levels didn't change, doctors began to look closer at the diagnosis, including using "new technology that had come out" around brain MRIs, she said.

In 2024, the official diagnostic criteria was updated after a committee of experts evaluated new scientific advances — including the use of new tools like advanced MRIs capable of more specific detection.
Ultimately, it was concluded Applegate didn't have MS — but she wasn't given another diagnosis to replace it, leaving her in the dark as to what was causing her ongoing symptoms.

"I feel like I let everybody down, you know?" Applegate said tearfully to co-host Sigler, saying she felt like they'd become "the poster children for MS" together. The two started their podcast in 2024, featuring conversations about parenting and ordinary life struggles while dealing with the disease.
"It's like I had a reason … for why my day sucked every day, and now I don't have a reason. It's very unnerving."

items: How an MS diagnosis made Ardra Shephard look at life differently

blocks.text: The actress, who stepped away from the screen in 2021 after her diagnosis, is known for roles in movies such as Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, and Bad Moms, and for TV roles including her Emmy-nominated turn in Netflix’s Dead to Me.
Global rates of MS

Globally, more than 3.1 million people are living with MS worldwide, according to MS International Federation. Canada has one of the highest rates of the disease in the world, with more than 90,000 Canadians, roughly one in 400, affected by it. Around seven out of 10 cases are among women.

It can be difficult to diagnose because many conditions have overlapping neurological and physical symptoms — for instance, migraines can also create white spots on an MRI of the brain, and nerve damage from other conditions can create numbness.
This McMaster study has participants with MS play Tetris

Being treated for MS when you don't actually have it can be risky for patients, Freedman said, as some of the more aggressive MS treatments work by suppressing the immune system, potentially exposing patients to viruses for no reason.
"The longer you take them and the older you are, the better the chances you're gonna have a problem," he said.

In Canada, he says, the misdiagnosis rate is much lower than in the U.S., estimating it at less than five per cent. He puts it down to Canada having a higher number of MS specialists and dedicated MS centres.

"What we teach our residents and fellows is if you're not sure of the diagnosis, you follow up the patients, you repeat testing, you look for the other thing that could look like MS, but you don't put the label on."

items: Researchers want to know how people with multiple sclerosis might be helped by playing Tetris
UBC researcher suggests multiple sclerosis may develop earlier than people think

blocks.text: In the podcast, Sigler reassured Applegate that her advocacy was still important even if she was misdiagnosed, and admitted that even if Applegate couldn't feel happy, her first thought on hearing the news had been that one day, her friend might be able to dance again.
"I'm going to continue holding in my heart that this is a blessing for you," Sigler said.

articles.title: Lebanon faces uncertainty as UNIFIL mandate nears end
articles.summary: As UN peacekeeping forces prepare to withdraw from Lebanon, Israel remains present and Hezbollah is still armed. A new EU support mission aims to strengthen Lebanon's army, but will not replace UN…

image.caption: Thousands of troops are due to leave Lebanon as the UNIFIL mandate ends on December 31, 2026, prompting fears of a security vacuum Image: Mahmoud Zayyat/AFP

blocks.text: As the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, nears its end, uncertainty over the future of southern Lebanon is growing. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has warned of the need to "avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it."

The Lebanese government has also been pushing for a last-minute extension of UNIFIL's mandate, but so far without success. It is most likely that the 7,565 peacekeepers from 46 countries will begin withdrawing from the UN-patrolled so-called Blue Line zone on December 31, 2026.

The Blue Line, which stretches for 120 kilometers (75 miles), is a UN-identified line of withdrawal between Israel and Lebanon, not an internationally agreed border. It was established in 2000. However, as early as in 1978, multinational UNIFIL troops were deployed to this region to monitor the area after Israel invaded Lebanon in response to attacks by Palestinian armed groups.

After the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war, the mandate was expanded to support the Lebanese army in implementing UN Security Council Resolution 1701. The resolution calls for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River to be free of armed personnel, assets and weapons other than those belonging to the Lebanese government and UNIFIL. It also calls for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.

However, following cross-border attacks by Hezbollah in October 2023 and the ensuing war in 2024, Israel has been occupying large swaths of Lebanese territory in a self-declared security zone called the Yellow Line, which is located north of the Blue Line.

Of the more than 1.2 million people displaced in Lebanon during the renewed conflict in 2026, around 329,000 remained internally displaced as of September 29, according to the International Organization for Migration. Israel has also caused extensive destruction to homes and key infrastructure in southern Lebanon, saying it needs to protect its citizens in northern Israel from attacks launched from the area.

Hezbollah — which is designated as a terrorist organization by several countries, including the United States and Germany, while the European Union designates its armed wing as a terrorist organization — continues to reject disarmament, citing the need to defend itself for as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.
Hezbollah is also closely linked to Iran, and in case of renewed conflict between Iran and Israel, it's likely that Hezbollah would open a second front in Israel's north in support of Iran.

blocks.caption: Around 1.2 million people were displaced in Lebanon this year. However, the majority have since returned to their homes in the southImage: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The situation in southern Lebanon remains tense," Kandice Ardiel, UNIFIL's spokesperson, told DW. "We are seeing continued Israeli military operations, including overflights of Lebanese airspace by jets, helicopters and drones, airstrikes, artillery strikes and mortar fire."

"Until our mandate ends on December 31, we continue to monitor and report what is happening, and we are liaising between the parties on a daily basis to ensure safe movements of civilians, humanitarian aid, and peacekeeping patrols," she said, adding that the drawdown and withdrawal would then take place in stages.

The end of the mandate also means the end of the mission for thousands of UNIFIL troops in southern Lebanon. "People have built careers, friendships, skills and a sense of purpose together," Ardiel said. "Endings are never easy, especially when there is a sense that the work we do is still needed."
Beirut's lack of authority, money compounds disarmament dilemma
The upcoming withdrawal of UNIFIL also highlights two major dilemmas for Lebanon's government.

"Beirut is concerned that violations of any agreements, whether on the Israeli or the Hezbollah side, can't be tracked in the absence of an international military force," Paul Shaya, a Washington-based Middle East researcher and adjunct professor at George Washington University, told DW.

Furthermore, after years of political deadlock, the COVID-19 pandemic, soaring inflation and economic crises, the Beirut port blast in 2020 and the destruction caused by the 2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah, Lebanon's economic lifeline depends on international funding. However, a large share of the much-needed investment from the United States and Gulf states is tied to Hezbollah's disarmament.
"Ultimately, it is going to be dependent on President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam to secure sufficient funding and resources to support the Lebanese military," said Shaya.
Can Lebanon's peace experiment work?

Until that happens, Aoun and Salam have very limited options for disarming Hezbollah, said David Wood, Lebanon researcher at the International Crisis Group. "They have opened direct talks with Israel to bring about an end to the disastrous conflict, but that process includes neither Hezbollah nor its backer Iran — both of which oppose the group's disarmament," he said.

In Wood's view, Beirut has few bargaining chips in negotiations with Israel because it has been unable to secure Hezbollah's compliance. He is also worried that Lebanon's leaders have little leverage to force Hezbollah to surrender its weapons, as this could trigger a deadly domestic conflict in the country. In the past, Hezbollah has openly warned that trying to seize its weapons by force would lead to war.

Despite Israel's destruction of many Hezbollah tunnels and weapons-storage facilities in Hezbollah-dominated areas in southern Lebanon and parts of Beirut, the limitation or disruption of supply routes due to the wider Iran war, as well as the fall of their ally, Syrian President Bashar Assad, observers say Hezbollah remains better equipped than the Lebanese armed forces.
Could the new EU mission replace UNIFIL in Lebanon?
On October 12, European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, with an initial three-year mandate.
"It has a civilian and military pillar," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, adding that "this is highly welcomed by the local authorities."

blocks.caption: The Iran-backed Hezbollah group maintains a political arm as well as a military arm in LebanonImage: Hussein Malla/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to the European Council, the mission is to contribute to peace and security in Lebanon by strengthening the capabilities of the Lebanese armed forces and internal security forces, including in border security in accordance with the UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
However, the mission is not intended to replace UNIFIL. Rather than deploying peacekeepers to patrol southern Lebanon, it is set to initially operate north of the Litani River.

Several existing UNIFIL contributors, including Italy, France, Spain, Ireland, Germany, Austria, Finland and Poland, already expressed interest in contributing personnel and resources to the new EUSM Lebanon mission.

For the government in Beirut, this is a positive signal, noted Shaya. He added that Lebanese society also strongly supports the Lebanese military, "which many see as the only institution in the country that can uphold Lebanon's sovereignty and represent the entire country."

articles.title: Sudan drone strike kills around 150 in Abyei market
articles.summary: A drone strike hit a market in the Abyei border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan and killed dozens. The drone caused a large fire when it hit a fuel depot. South Sudanese officials blamed…

image.caption: Medical workers, including from Medecins Sans Frontieres, worked to treat the wounded at the nearby Ameth Bek hospitalImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: A drone strike in a busy market in the disputed region of Abyei has killed more than 150 people, according to local officials.

South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military for the attack, without providing evidence, amid the long-running civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which is reportedly active in the Abyei area.

The special UN mission in Abyei warned in May that the RSF's presence in the resource-rich region had put residents in additional danger, and risked intensifying the older territorial dispute between Sudan and the world's newest sovereign state, South Sudan.

blocks.caption: Satellite images gave a sense of the scale of the damage after the large fire triggered by the drone strikesImage: Planet Labs PBC/REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about the drone strike?
According to local authorities, the attack hit the busy Amiet Market at around midday on Monday.

Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker information minister in Abyei, told Reuters news agency on Tuesday that the death toll had more than doubled, reaching at least 153 compared to a stated figure of 73 the previous day.
He said that Sudan's military was responsible for the attack but did not provide evidence. Akol Ngor said around 8,000 people had been displaced by the bombing.
South Sudan's Foreign Ministry also blamed the Sudanese army and said the drone struck multiple locations around the busy market.
One of these, judging by witness accounts, was a fuel depot — and this led to a large fire that proved difficult to bring under control overnight and was still ablaze on Tuesday.
South Sudan said it had summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to "refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property."
Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders, said that its staff was treating some 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek hospital.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted," said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF's medical activities manager at the hospital.

blocks.caption: Many of the wounded were taken to Ameth Bek hospital for treatmentImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's the backstory of Sudan, South Sudan and Abyei?
The oil-rich Abyei region's status was not resolved by the 2005 peace agreement that broadly ended decades of civil war in Sudan.
It was also not settled in 2011 when South Sudan became an independent country.

A referendum was planned but never materialized, stalling over disputes on who should be allowed to vote. This left Abyei in a state of limbo, jointly administered and with an interim UN security force on site for 15 years.
The region's majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan.
Amiet Market, the site of the attack, is an important trading hub for both communities.
The unstable region has also experienced intercommunal violence in recent years between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities and is home to other armed militias.

blocks.caption: Medecins Sans Frontieres said its staff were providing surgical services, wound dressing and other emergency care to more than 20 woundedImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: How does this fit into Sudan's army's war with the RSF?

The April 2023 outbreak of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary — which has turned into a conflict with fairly entrenched battle lines, putting Sudan into a de facto state of partition — is increasing tension in the already-strained region.
Abyei borders South Kordofan state in Sudan, which has become a major center of fighting in the war.
Sudan's military alleges that the RSF is also operating out of Abyei. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) issued a similar statement in May.
Officials in Abyei and South Sudan dispute this, however.
Sudan's military and the RSF have both been using drones extensively in the conflict.

"We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure — these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters in New York on Tuesday when asked about the attack.
Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid

articles.title: North Korean workers treated as 'slaves' at Russian drone factory
articles.summary: A new report reveals the plight of North Korean workers at a drone factory in Russia. It also raised concerns that Pyongyang could gain hands-on knowledge of advanced weapons systems through the…

image.caption: North Korean state media showed Kim Jong Un inspecting drones at an undisclosed location in North Korea (FILE: September 2026)Image: KCNA/KNS/AFP

blocks.text: As many as 12,000 North Koreans working at a Russian drone factory are victims of "gross human rights abuses and human trafficking," according to a new report.

The figures were part of a joint report published on October 14 by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the Dallas-based George W. Bush Institute. It analyzes how Russia, North Korea, China and Iran are involved in expanding unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) production at the Yelabuga plant in Tatarstan, and what each country stands to gain.

While Moscow gets access to more than 5,500 drones a month for its war against Ukraine, China benefits from being the main supplier of dual-use components, including batteries, internal electronics, engines and navigation systems.
Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drones, which has helped Moscow produce upgraded domestic variants, known as Geran.
Meanwhile, North Korea is earning money by retaining as much as 90% of the wages of the laborers, the report stated.

"The geographical locations of these four countries… means that any kind of international interdiction is impossible," Dan Pinkston, a professor of international relations at the Seoul campus of Troy University, told DW.
North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine
Russia and North Korea defy UN resolutions

The joint report says Russia and North Korea are defying United Nations Security Council Resolution 2397, of December 2017, which requires any UN member state to send North Korean workers home within two years.

"The North Korean regime… is selling the labor of its citizens under a state-to-state arrangement, controlling whether they may leave and collecting most of their wages," it said. This, according to the report, "is the definition of forced labor."

Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist with the Worldwide Coalition to Stop Genocide in North Korea, says Pyongyang is "effectively conducting slavery of its own people and for its own profit."

"This is just a terrible situation, and we know that it is not happening only at Yelabuga," he told DW. "We know there are construction workers in the occupied Ukrainian territories, North Koreans in lumber camps and, of course, tens of thousands of soldiers have been sent to fight — and die — on the front lines in Ukraine," Song added.
"Life in North Korea is not easy, but these people are being sent to Russia as slaves, with no freedom, and they are only allowed to keep a fraction of the money they earn," he said.
The challenge, he admits, is to find a way to halt this "trade in humanity."
North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine
How much can realistically be done?

"These countries share a border, so it is easy to transport workers, and no other agency can intervene," Song said. "Russia and China are both permanent members of the UN Security Council but are ignoring its resolutions on this issue. There is very little that can be done."

Song's rights organization is attempting to highlight the plight of North Korean workers and to create a "coalition of like-minded nations and agencies" to protect laborers — although he admits to being "pessimistic."

Pinkston shares those concerns, as well as fears over the emergence of a powerful bloc that appears to be "ripping up the post-World War II order on the rule of law and human rights" and is intent on taking a confrontational approach to other nations.
The weapons being manufactured at Yelabuga will assist in achieving those aims, he said.

"UN Security Council resolutions on North Korean workers, on weapons proliferation, on the sale of dual-use technologies are all being ignored, so I think we can say that the UN's sanctions regime is pretty much dead," Pinkston added.
North Korea developing its drone capabilities

It is clear that both Russia and Ukraine have gained important insights into the modern battlefield through their ongoing conflict, Pinkston said, with the emergence of drone technology arguably one of the most critical advances.

"And like everyone else, North Korea has been watching closely, 'learning-by-doing' and innovating its own drone capabilities," Pinkston said, adding that there are "serious implications" for the South Korean military as it also attempts to keep up its defensive capabilities against a new generation of drones in the North.
Why Russia and North Korea can't quit each other (for now)

To curb the deployment of North Korean laborers to Russia and the proliferation of weapons, the joint report calls on the US State Department to work with other countries to disrupt human trafficking networks and sanction those responsible.

It also urges the UN to work multilaterally to investigate the Yelabuga complex and to catalogue the abuses that have taken place. Moreover, it demands accountability for those who have carried out abuses and for victims to be protected.

The report adds that foreign companies that are operating as part of the Yelabuga special economic zone — there are "several" European companies and at least one US firm with a presence at the site — should be pressured to leave.

articles.title: Satellite images reveal Wainwright, Alta., fire devastation
articles.summary: The charred land where a blaze ripped through a portion of CFB Wainwright and claimed the lives of four service members in Alberta on Saturday can be seen from space.

image.caption: The burned area on CFB Wainwright on Monday. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada
The charred land where a blaze ripped through a portion of CFB Wainwright and claimed the lives of four service members in Alberta on Saturday can be seen from space.
Charred landscape following deadly blaze can be seen from space
The charred land where a blaze ripped through a portion of CFB Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday, claiming the lives of four service members and injuring dozens of others, can be seen from space.

Images from Planet Labs shows the extent of the fire, which was fuelled at least in part by dry land and howling winds. Environment Canada had issued a wind alert that morning and the fire danger index in the area was deemed extreme by Natural Resources Canada.

The images show a burnt area of roughly 10 square kilometres on Sunday, one day after the blaze was first reported. The general area of the base where the fire began is referred to as a "permanent danger area" by OpenStreetMap, a widely used geographic database maintained by volunteers.
On Sunday, the Municipal District of Wainwright reported the fire was being held.

Canadian Armed Forces Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, inaugural commander of the revitalized 1st Canadian Division, told reporters Sunday that the fire began as a grass fire and spread rapidly around 4 p.m. as the wind direction changed.
That day, soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a grenade range, he said, while others were conducting a "section attack," in which 10 soldiers attack a simulated enemy.

articles.title: New EU plan for Arctic warily eyes influence of Russia, US
articles.summary: The EU unveiled its priorities in the Arctic as it vies with Russia, China and the US for influence. EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage…

image.caption: Greenland's melting ice sheet is a climate risk which is contributing to global sea level rise [FILE: May 5, 2021]Image: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: The EU on Tuesday presented a new Arctic Strategy that outlines the bloc's priorities in the key region amid challenges such as security threats, climate change and mining.

Russia is building up its military power in the Arctic, and US President Donald Trump has threatened Greenland, saying the Danish territory is needed for American security interests but later signed a deal with Denmark over US military access to the territory. China is also investing in the region and has shipping ambitions there.

The northern parts of Finland and Sweden, along with Greenland are located within the Arctic, meaning part of the region is in the European neighborhood. Iceland and Norway, two other Arctic states, are also involved in the European single market.
'Tectonic plates of geopolitics' colliding in Arctic
"The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

"When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned security in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture," she added.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia "has reopened Soviet-era bases and is testing new weapons" in the Arctic.

"Drone incursions, GPS jamming and the sabotage of undersea cables undermine Arctic security," Kallas continued. Russia's shadow fleet, which is an attempt to circumvent Western sanctions, is active in the Arctic.

On Arctic security, the EU plans to develop a maritime security hub in the region "to facilitate information sharing form seabed to space." The bloc also intends to expand European icebreaker capacity and extend its satellite surveillance program in the region.
Russia's Arctic buildup is Iceland's security headache
However, the EU does not intend to compete with NATO in the region, EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela told DW. Twenty-three EU countries are members of NATO.

"NATO will remain basically the center of defense and the center of deterrence, but NATO doesn't have a budget, the member state has," Sikela said. "This is first about the proper focus and the proper use of resources of the NATO member states and about better coordination."
EU Arctic strategy highlights security and raw materials
EU to boost climate research as Arctic faces ice melting crisis

In regard to the climate, the Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average. The melting of ice and glaciers in the Arctic pose risks to Europe such as prolonged heatwaves, drought and flooding.
Sikela said, "Collaboration among the Arctic is very difficult," adding, "We're not getting information about the permafrost from the biggest part of the Arctic territory."

Sikela accused Russia of "unprecedented" actions in the Arctic and said the "catastrophic level of drilling and opening new mines" in the region is contributing to its rapid warming. The Arctic is rich in critical minerals and rare earth elements such as nickel.

As part of the EU Arctic Strategy, the bloc intends "to strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring" and launch flagship projects utilizing AI to "anticipate extreme weather and cascading disasters such as coastal flooding."

blocks.caption: Norway, which is not an EU member state, is home to Western Europe's largest LNG plant near the city of Hammerfest  [FILE: March 14, 2024]Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS

blocks.text: Although Russia and other non-EU countries such as Norway drill in the Arctic, the EU does not want to expand new drilling in the region. European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said the EU's view "on drilling in the Arctic remains the same and it's very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground."
Greenland submarine cable route project bypasses US

Regarding economic interests in the Arctic, the bloc may take further steps to bypass the US. The strategy calls for "resilient submarine cable connectivity linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions towards Canada and Japan."
The EU also outlined new plans regarding the residents of the Arctic region. The bloc wants to strengthen dialogue with Indigenous people along with expanding Erasmus+ opportunities for Arctic youth.
Denmark apologizes for abuse of Greenlandic Indigenous women

articles.title: ‘Bad decisions’: Man convicted for taking Peachy the flamingo from Las Vegas hotel
articles.summary:
Mitchell Fairbarn found guilty of animal cruelty after prosecutors say he hurt and frightened the 27-year-old bird

A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching…

blocks.text: A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges on Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its enclosure at an iconic Las Vegas hotel.
Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for the tourist insisted it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird.

Prosecutors said tourist Mitchell Fairbarn hurt and frightened the 27-year-old Chilean flamingo when he took it from its habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino and carried the squawking bird to his room on 3 March. Defense attorney Josh Tomsheck told jurors at trial in a Nevada court that the man deeply regretted the “bad decisions” he made while intoxicated.
After about five hours of deliberations, jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts against the Ontario, Canada, man.

Fairbarn remains under house arrest pending a sentencing hearing set for 1 December. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony and possibly six more months for the misdemeanor conviction. Following the verdict, he declined to comment as he left the courtroom with his wife. He showed no visible emotion.
His lawyer also had no comment.

After the incident, the flamingo was mostly unharmed but is more anxious and nervous when being evaluated, said Peachy’s veterinarian, Tiffany Moore, medical director of Lone Mountain Animal Hospital.

Prosecutors told jurors earlier that Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor. Video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it and prosecutors said Peachy felt pain when it was pulled by its feet.

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway at the famous hotel. The Flamingo is one of the oldest hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and its well-known flamingo habitat also features hummingbirds, turtles, koi and other species.
Peachy was missing some feathers after being taken.

Las Vegas police responded to the scene after security staff reported that someone had taken the flamingo. When Peachy was located, it was missing seven to eight feathers, had blood on its feathers and injuries to its wings, authorities said.
Taking the bird was “dumb” and “fueled by drunkenness”, the defense attorney Tomsheck said. But he added that his client never intended any harm to the bird, a key element in the felony charge.

“He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn’t have touched a bird, shouldn’t have taken Peachy inside,” Tomsheck said. “The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions.”
Fairbarn could be seen in court at one point with head lowered, hands covering his eyes.

The man had received death threats after taking the flamingo, and he was unable to leave the US when his father died while Fairbarn was awaiting trial, said Haley Willming, the Clark county prosecutor. While those events were unfortunate, the prosecutor said, “none of that would have happened had he not done what he did, had he not made the choices he made”.
Jurors began deliberating shortly before midday after closing arguments on Monday morning.
Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state’s animal cruelty laws, said he believes justice was delivered on Peachy’s behalf.
“I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you’re not going to do it in Nevada,” he said outside the courtroom after Monday’s verdict.

articles.title: EDCOM 2 cites gaps in classroom allocations
articles.summary: The Second Congressional Commission on Education found gaps in the distribution of classroom allocations, with some municipalities with the largest shortages allegedly receiving fewer classrooms.

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 12:00am
EDCOM 2 said the issue was raised during the Oct. 16 Senate committee on finance hearing on the Department of Education (DepEd)’s proposed budget for 2027.
EDCOM 2

MANILA, Philippines — The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) found gaps in the distribution of classroom allocations, with some municipalities with the largest shortages allegedly receiving fewer classrooms.

EDCOM 2 reportedly discovered that in DepEd’s 2026 classroom allocation, only 45.2 percent of the 332 local governments with the largest estimated classroom shortages were among the top recipients of planned classroom allocations.

EDCOM 2 co-chairman Sen. Bam Aquino said DepEd and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) should accelerate classroom construction and ensure that allocations translate into completed facilities.

For this year, DepEd has initiated multiple channels to speed up classroom construction, targeting to complete 18,950 classrooms. It tapped the DPWH, partnered with provincial and city governments, civil society organizations and Public-Private Partnership Programs (PPPs).

EDCOM 2 executive director Karol Mark Yee praised DepEd for its “extraordinary efforts in mobilizing different routes for classroom construction. However, we also highlight the need for strategic and responsive allocations to ensure that these resources go where they are most needed.”

The commission reported that seven of the 10 municipalities with the highest funds for 2026 classroom construction received allocations exceeding their estimated classroom shortages based on 2023 data. Meanwhile, several municipalities with substantial deficits remained short of the classrooms needed to accommodate their learners.

“For instance, Maragondon, Cavite was allocated 272 classrooms against an estimated shortage of just 64. In contrast, Tanza, Cavite, received 448 classrooms against a shortage of a whopping 869, while Naic, Cavite was allocated 356 against a deficit of 631,” it explained.
EDCOM 2 also raised concerns over delays in classroom construction, particularly under DPWH-led implementation.

Out of the P21.45-billion allocation for 6,000 DPWH-led classrooms under the FY 2026 program, only P1.87 billion, covering 533 classrooms, allegedly reached the award or near-award stage during the hearing. Another P7 billion, covering approximately 2,000 classrooms, had been advertised for procurement.
DPWH Undersecretary Lara Esquibil pointed to failed biddings and higher construction costs amid rising fuel prices as factors affecting the implementation.
EDCOM 2 is reportedly creating a classroom tracker for transparency on where the funds are going.

For 2027, the National Expenditure Program (NEP) reportedly proposes P30.55 billion for classroom construction, with an additional request of P23.5 billion from DepEd for the construction of 2,385 new classrooms, 69 Last Mile School buildings, 500 Learning Continuity Spaces, as well as repair of 3,500 classrooms, among others. — Neil Jayson Servallos

articles.title: Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
articles.summary: Janine Lochrenberg, 65, was out on her daily morning swim with her club when she was attacked, her family tell the BBC.

blocks.text: A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.
Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.
Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.
Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.

Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.
She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.
Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.
She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London".
"She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.
Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave.
"She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."
Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.
Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoff
articles.summary:
Far-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody it

To Flávio Bolsonaro and his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious…

blocks.text: To Flávio Bolsonaro and his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious idea that would expose his rival’s supposed crookedness on the eve of Brazil’s presidential election.

But the far-right politician’s decision to attend a primetime television debate against his leftwing opponent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with the word “corrupto” (corrupt) written on the palm of his hand has backfired.
Rather than drawing attention to the incumbent’s alleged misdeeds, many of the programme’s millions of viewers sarcastically took Bolsonaro’s hand-written message as an admission of his own guilt.
Following Sunday night’s debate, Lula supporters from all walks of life have flooded social media with photographs of their own self-descriptions inked on their palms.
John Ulhoa, the guitarist from a pop rock band called Pato Fu, jokingly described himself as a “musician (and a hunk)”.
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.
The Emmy-winning comedian Antonio Tabet introduced himself to his 2.8 million followers on X as an artist.
Carlos Marcio used both palms to portray himself as a cellist and author.
Carla Emanuela Sacramento, an obstetric nurse, posted a photograph of herself clad in personal protective equipment and with the words “primary health care nurse” proudly written on her right palm.

Prominent politicians also jumped on the trend, including Lula’s health minister, the infectious disease specialist Alexandre Padilha, whose palm noted he was a doctor, and Tabata Amaral, who identified as a political scientist and astrophysicist.

All across the country, librarians, oil workers, engineers, journalists, architects, pilots, psychologists, seamstresses, street cleaners, teachers, influencers, and police officers used ballpoint pens to inscribe their professions on to their skin.
Writing on Substack, the Latin America expert James Bosworth called Bolsonaro’s stunt a “critical error” in his bid for power.

“It may have seemed like an inspired pre-debate gimmick. Instead, he gave the world a meme image that will stick with him for the rest of his political career,” Bosworth said, offering politicians a word of advice.
“Don’t write the word ‘corrupto’ on your hand and show it to the audience,” Bosworth suggested.

Bolsonaro, who is the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, is a professional politician who has long faced corruption accusations, although he denies them and has never been convicted. The 45-year-old senator also has well-documented ties to members of Rio’s mafia underworld and once employed the relatives of the city’s most notorious contract killer, Adriano da Nóbrega. Last week two allies were arrested for alleged involvement with the Red Command drug faction, which Donald Trump recently designated a foreign terrorist organisation. Bolsonaro voiced surprise at those arrests and said the men had the right to prove their innocence.
On Monday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro was being investigated by the federal police as part of a money-laundering inquiry.
Lula, whose Worker’s party (PT) has also been involved in major corruption scandals, used Sunday’s debate to throw down the gauntlet to Bolsonaro.

The leftwing incumbent said he would give electoral authorities access to his banking and phone recordings, and those of close relatives, in order to prove he was not corrupt – if Bolsonaro agreed to do the same.

Bolsonaro, who, polls suggest, holds a slender advantage ahead of Sunday’s second-round runoff, has yet to respond to Lula’s challenge. The rightwinger won the 4 October first round by more than 2m votes.

articles.title: Germany news: Hackers release AfD party emails
articles.summary: Germany's far-right AfD has launched an inquiry after the release of thousands of emails following a cyberattack. Also, investors pledged billions for Germany at a major summit in Berlin. DW has more…

image.caption: The released material reportedly included emails sent by party figures as well as bank statements, academic certificates and membership listsImage: Felix Kästle/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Published October 20, 2026last updated October 20, 2026
Far-right AfD says emails stolen in September cyberattack

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) said on Tuesday that it was looking into the theft and subsequent online publication of emails stolen by unidentified hackers during a cyberattack last month.
An AfD spokesperson said the hackers had targeted a hosting provider used by the party and appeared to have copied data from a small number of mostly inactive email accounts.

"The recent online publication of what is presumably a portion of this data is currently being investigated," the spokesperson said. "A preliminary assessment can only be provided once this investigation has been concluded."
Although the spokesperson did not say how much data was stolen, an earlier report by the mass-circulation daily Bild put the number of AfD-linked emails published at more than 420,000.
According to Bild, the material published included not only emails sent by party figures such as co-leader Alice Weidel but also bank statements, academic certificates and membership lists.
The website hosting the material was offline by Tuesday afternoon.
However, archived versions showed a volume of 281 gigabytes of data under the headline "The party's own records, unedited."
The emails and other materials published have not yet been certified as authentic by any independent body.

The AfD, several state chapters of which have been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by regional branches of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, has been topping recent national opinion polls and made gains in recent state elections.
Some politicians and civil society groups have called for it to be banned, arguing that the party is a threat to democracy, an accusation the party has rejected.

articles.title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 200 people, sources say
articles.summary: A truck carrying people to a funeral and a market alleged to be supplying fuel to the RSF were targeted.
articles.byline: Richard Kagoe, Lucy Fleming, Richard Irvine-Brown

blocks.text: Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 200 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.

The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
